utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Madam Judge. Good day, Your Honour. Good day, Mr. President. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, I'm accompanied by Mr. Alexis Demirdjian today, our legal assistant, and an interpreter for the team who can enable us to communicate with Mr. Hadzihasanovic if necessary in the course of Mr. Duncan's testimony. Vedrana Residovic is the name of the interpreter, and I am Stephane Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, and our registrar, who has returned to us. I will now give the floor to Mr. Withopf, who will inform us of the witness we will be hearing. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution will call the witness Alastair Duncan. I anticipate, as already announced yesterday by Mr. Mundis, that the examination-in-chief will last about 1 hour 30 minutes, maybe 1 hour 45 minutes. And I intend to use the following documents: Exhibits P225, P216, P162, and DH72. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. Madam Usher has gone to bring the witness into the courtroom. We are waiting for him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day. I would like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I am saying into your own language. If so, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've been called here to testify about events that took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993. You've been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. Before giving your testimony, you must take the solemn declaration. But before you read out the solemn declaration, could you tell me your first and last names. THE WITNESS: My name is Alastair Duncan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me your date of birth, your place of birth, and your nationality, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on the 22nd of October, 1952 at Toft Monks in Norfolk in England, and I'm English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What rank and what position do you currently hold?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Major general, general de division. And I'm currently commanding Land Warfare Centre in the British Army which is responsible for all military training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What duties did you perform and what rank did you have in 1993, over ten years ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1993, I was a lieutenant colonel, the commanding officer of the 1st Battalion, the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire. And I was based in Osnabruck in Germany as an armoured infantry battalion. But I was deployed to Bosnia, to the Lasva Valley area, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international or national court about the events of 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I've been here twice before, once for the court case against Tihomir Blaskic and once for the court case against Dario Kordic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. You've may sit down now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, before the Prosecution commences its examination-in-chief I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure followed here. As you have already testified in other cases, you are already used to the procedure followed. Initially you will have to answer questions put to you by representatives of the Prosecution, who are to your right. And you have already met them. Once this stage has been completed - it should take between an hour and a half and an hour and 45 minutes - and after our break, you will be cross-examined. The cross-examination will be conducted by Defence counsel for the accused. Two members of the Defence counsel will conduct the cross-examination, the purpose of which is to verify the credibility of the witness and also to clarify certain issues that might make the situation at the time clearer. Once the cross-examination has been completed, the Prosecution will take the floor again to ask you additional questions, which will be based on the questions put to you in the course of the cross-examination. The three Judges who are sitting before you may ask you questions and will ask you questions at any point in time. As a general rule, the Judges prefer to wait for the examination-in-chief, the cross-examination, and re-examination to be concluded, after which they ask a witness questions. The purpose of the Judges' questions is to clarify answers that you have provided to the parties or to obtain additional information if necessary and to fill in any gaps they might feel they have noticed in your answers. Once the Judges have asked you their questions, both parties may ask you additional questions. This hearing will go on until about 1.45, but if we don't have time to complete the hearing, it will continue tomorrow. Sometimes the questions might be a little confusing, but try to provide precise and clear answers to the extent that this is possible. The Judges don't have any documents relating to your testimony, and as a result we will be counting on your oral testimony to understand the events in question. As the proceedings are oral, it's necessary for the questions and answers to be as clear as possible for the Judges. I would like to inform you of two other factors: You have just taken the solemn declaration, which means that you should not give false testimony. False testimony is punishable. And there is another provision which shouldn't apply to you, but I would like to point out that if a witness answers a question and the answer could be used to prosecute the witness at a subsequent date, in such a case the witness can refuse to answer the question. If a witness refuses to answer such a question, the Trial Chamber can compel the witness to answer, but the witness benefits from a form of immunity in such a case. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. So generally speaking this is how the hearing will proceed. Without wasting any more time, I will let the Prosecution -- I will let Mr. Withopf take the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber briefly summarise your military career within the British Army from the time you joined it up until now, with the emphasis on deployments abroad, if any.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Certainly. I joined the British Army in 1970, and I have commanded at every level on operations and in training, at platoon, a company, battalion, brigade, and division. In particular, I served on operations in Northern Ireland as a platoon commander, a company commander, and a battalion commander, and then in the Balkans as a battalion commander and later as deputy commander of the multinational division in Banja Luka, which I took over, a short time, as the divisional commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already mentioned it, sir, but for the sake of the transcript, can you please again inform us about your military rank whilst deployed in Central Bosnia in 1993.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: In 1993, I was a lieutenant colonel, commanding an armoured infantry battalion which was based in Osnabruck in Germany. I had been in command for two and a half years before we deployed to Bosnia. And I then deployed with my entire battle group, consisting of armoured vehicles and Land Rovers, to the area of the Lasva Valley. And in slightly more detail, I had a company based in Gornji Vakuf, I had two companies based on the Nova Bila School north of Vitez, and a company in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And, sir, what's your rank today?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: My rank today is as major general.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, can you please inform us briefly about your current duties.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I'm currently commanding the Land Warfare Centre, which is based on Salisbury Plain in the UK. My responsibilities are for pre-employment training for individuals, so officers and soldiers prior to taking over a specific appointment will come through my organisation for training. More importantly, I am responsible for the training of the entire British Army for operations. So every single soldier from the British Army who deploys on operations will come through my organisation of collective training before they deploy. I have training bases in the UK on Salisbury Plain; in Canada, at Alberta; at Belize; at Kenya; and in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, let's talk about your deployment in Central Bosnia in 1993. Can you please inform the Trial Chamber from when to when and in what exact function you were deployed in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I deployed as the commanding officer of the British Battalion, which was part of UNPROFOR, from May till November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Prior to being deployed with BritBat in Central Bosnia, did you travel in the area for reconnaissance purposes?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I did two reconnaissances before deploying with my battalion many May. The first was, if I remember, the last week in January, and then about three weeks later I came back with a much fuller team for another week for a second reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In addition to your two reconnaissance missions prior to being deployed, did you receive a further briefing prior to taking over command of BritBat?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. I came out somewhat earlier than would be normal. In the British Army, it is normal that the commanding officer - who at that time was Colonel Bob Stewart - and I would change over when I had more soldiers in theatre than he had, and we'd normally change over like that. However, because of the complex nature of the task I was given in Bosnia, I decided to deploy some six days earlier. This gave me the chance to go round the whole of the British Battalion area, less Tuzla, to meet not only the people who were doing the job on the ground but also to meet representatives from the BiH and the HVO that I would be working with for the next six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, would it be fair to say that at the point in time you took over command of BritBat on the 11th of May, 1993 you were already fully aware of the military situation in the area of responsibility of BritBat?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That would be entirely true. I'd spent a great deal of time. They were very long day, those six days, out first thing in the morning and back last thing at night, and then following on a series of discussions about things I'd seen and heard during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already mentioned it, but for the sake of the transcript can you please inform the Trial Chamber where exactly you were based whilst you were the commanding officer of BritBat.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I was based in the school in Nova Bila, which was formerly obviously a local school. We set up base there. I had my headquarters there with two companies. And further down the road, I think there was a location we called the garage towards Vitez, was where my echelon, which was responsible for replying and sustaining the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And, General, can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the chain of command within BritBat and the structure. How was the operation organised?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: We kept our normal chain of command. I was required to report directly to UNPROFOR in Kiseljak. That is unusual in the British Army, that you go straight through from battalion right through to what is effectively a theatre headquarters. And UNPROFOR was laid out with a series of battalions across Bosnia at that stage, each with a unique area, but each, I believe, with a common task of making sure that aid was delivered. That command structure, then, I was given direction from Kiseljak, came down to me, and in turn I gave orders down to my company commanders, and they were responsible for organising the patrolling below that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, you already touched on it briefly. Can you please inform us about your mission whilst deployed in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: My mission was to create the conditions whereby aid could be distributed into and through my area of responsibility. This mission I kept very short and simple. The reason for that was that it was very important that every single soldier under my command understood what my mission was. As we were so widely dispersed, it was very important that they were able to take decisions when out of contact. And the rule was if what I'm going to do is to help my commanding officer and his mission, then I can do it; if what I'm about to do would not help him, then I shouldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform us, General, about the essentials and the keys to guarantee the success of your mission.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I considered that to guarantee success of my mission I had to know exactly what was going on in my area, and so I established an information-gathering system across the whole of my area. And it was based on a series of levels, the first level being myself as commanding officer, the senior officer in the battalion, talking directly to the senior commanders of the BiH and the HVO, and it was important that I was seen to be speaking to them because they were influential people. So that was what I called the first level of gathering information. Below that I had my company commanders who were responsible for various areas within my area of responsibility, and they would deal with the brigade commanders from the HVO and BiH. That is the second level. The third level was achieved with about eight or nine young captains who were deployed out to specific formations within the two armies that were deployed there or to areas. And that was the third level of information gathering. The fourth level was done by patrols on the ground either in Land Rovers or the Warrior armoured vehicles that we had, and they gathered information as well. That information was then all brought back to my military information cell in Vitez and put together by my military information officer. And he was responsible for collating that information and, if necessary, making comment on what it thought. As a result of that, I was able to get a complete picture of what was going on in my area in order that I could influence events, ensure my mission of getting aid through was complete, and know what was going on if possible to pre-empt any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, General, that you had a complete intelligence-gathering system that was covering all military aspects within the area of responsibility of BritBat?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That would be correct, but I would add that I also had relationships with the UNHCR as well; and we also, if you like, plugged into some of the local dignitaries, the mayors of towns, normally it was my captains. So what I was trying to do was pick up every scrap of information I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was the information-gathering system you just described in very detail, was it already in place when you arrived in Central Bosnia in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Parts of it were in place, and in particular the young captains were in place. But I don't think my predecessor had actually formally defined it. I should add another reason why I formally decided -- my apologies -- why I formally designed the system was prevent other people within the United Nations coming -- who may have come into my area, if you like, upsetting things. And I told them, "Please do not come in and upset things." And to give you an example, sir, if I may: On one occasion I discovered that three different agencies had visited prison in Zenica from the UN. That was clearly ridiculous and upsetting the prison. So with this system I was able to make sure that the right person was talking to the right person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Based on this, would it be fair to say that it was a very effective information-gathering system?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I think it was very effective, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you immediately, after your arrival, implement the intelligence-gathering system you just described?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was something we had discussed back in Germany after my reconnaissances with my company commanders. We designed the system then with the knowledge of the area and the problems of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And was this system in place throughout the six months you were deployed in the area?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were you, as the commanding officer of BritBat, were you satisfied with the results this intelligence-gathering system produced?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I was satisfied that the system gave me what I believed to be the best possible knowledge of what was going on, very satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were the commanding officer of BritBat, did you have a system of daily meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: We had a system of meetings at 6.00, 1800 hours every evening, where the liaison officers, the young captains I'd sent out, the company commanders, the intelligence and military-information officers, in fact everybody, would gather in the conference room when there would be a full debrief of the day's activities from every level. So I would explain what I'd done; the company commanders at the second level, third level, fourth level would all go through what had happened in their area. This was to enable what was going on. Of course, some people missed that meeting because they were unavoidably detained elsewhere. But as a result of the meeting we produced a formal report for the day, a milinfosum. And this was put together every day as a formal document and sent to the various agencies in the UN, and sideways to our sister battalions in the UN and also to the UK. This ensured that everybody, whether they were at the meeting or not, firstly knew what had gone on that day; secondly, knew what we were doing about it; and thirdly, had some idea of my plans and ideas for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, who at the time was responsible for putting together the milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: On my -- within my battalion in Germany, I had an intelligence officer who was trained in the UK. He was a very bright young captain called Simon Harrison, and I immediately knew that he was the right person to run this organisation, and he headed up my military information cell and collated all this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Captain Simon Harrison, was he a trained, a professional, and an experienced intelligence officer?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Very much so, yes. Not only had he been on the course in the UK for all intelligence officers, but he had been working with me and my battle group for the last 18 months. So he knew how we worked and we had worked together as a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What are your views, General, first in respect to the skills of Captain Simon Harrison; and second, in respect to the quality of his analysis?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: He was a very intelligent and bright officer. Sadly, he has left the army and gone on to greater things in civilian life. But his power of analysis was enormous. He had a very good brain. He was able to remember scraps of information and put them together to come to some opinion and conclusions and analysis, which I found hugely helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I understand, General, that the information which was shared during the 1800-hour meetings became part of the milinfosums. Was there anything else what was incorporated in the milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: There were two parts in the milinfosum: The first part was the facts which were outlined. And then under the title "Comment," was either mine or Captain Simon Harrison's opinion of what this meant. So whilst the facts were there, we also made an opinion, and clearly the opinion was based on facts but it was not facts itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was the purpose, sir, what was the purpose of the milinfosums? Who was supposed to read the milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Everyone was supposed to read them at some stage. That might be the next morning if they came in. But it was to enable the maximum amount of knowledge as to what was going on across my command to get down to everybody. It was -- I felt it was very important that everybody knew what we were doing with our successes and failures, and it was to convey information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to whom were the milinfosums disseminated?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: They were disseminated down within my command through the normal command structure and to all those captains and the layers I've talked about. They were also sent to the battle groups or battalions in my area, the Canadian in particular. And they were sent off to Kiseljak to the UN headquarters. And a final copy went back to the UK to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did the warring factions get to know about the contents of the milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: They were the subject of the milinfosums, so they probably knew what was in them. But it wasn't usual to disclose what we put in them for the main reason of the comment, because whilst the comment wasn't fact, it was what we were thinking. And sometimes I thought that would be inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To conclude this line of questioning, General, would you consider the information which was contained in the milinfosums as reliable information?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I would say it was reliable information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, let's move on to a different subject, namely the military situation within the 3rd Corps -- ABiH 3rd Corps area of responsibility, in particular the ABiH-HVO conflict. My first question is, General: What was actually the geographical area of responsibility of BritBat?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: BritBat was responsible effectively from the Lasva Valley, running from Travnik and slightly to the west of that, where the Serbs were -- had a front line, and then across the entire valley as far as what call the Zenica flyover, which was a considerable way down towards Kiseljak. The area also extended north to take in Zenica. And beyond that we had a route north up to Tuzla, but the Tuzla company was very much independent. To the south-west we had the road which ran from Travnik down to Gornji Vakuf, where my last company was based, and that is where the area went down. But I think officially the area went down as far as what I believe is a placed called Romboci, which is above some lakes lower down on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was there an overlap between the AOR of ABiH 3rd Corps and BritBat? And if so, to what extent?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: There was a considerable overlap between the ABiH 3rd Corps and British Battalion, particularly in Travnik and Zenica. If you like, their forces were -- and in Gornji Vakuf -- their forces were around the Lasva Valley area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How would you describe, sir, for the information of the Trial Chamber, the military situation within the area of responsibility of ABiH 3rd Corps at the time you arrived in May 1993 in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: When I arrived, I think the incident at Ahmici had occurred some 10, 15 days before, where a number of Muslims had been killed, almost certainly by HVO forces. As a result of this, the delicate balance between the BiH and the HVO in the Lasva Valley was very much under threat and starting to crumble. At that stage, I think it would be fair to say that the HVO were the dominant partner of the two partners running there, but this began to change as the BiH were hugely upset about, if you like, being let down by their ally. They had worked extremely well together against the Serbs, but this fracture that occurred was starting to break down that balance of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were saying, General, that first it was the HVO who was the dominant military force and then later on the situation changed. Would it be fair to say that at some point in time the ABiH -- the ABiH 3rd Corps became the predominant or the dominant military force?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That, I believe, would be fair to say, in that during the six months I was there there was a steady and continuous advance by the 3rd Corps, until they became at the end of my tour very much the dominant partner, as it were, in this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, you are using the term "dominant military force." What is implied by saying "the dominant military force"?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: What I imply by that is they were the ones, put in vernacular, who were running the show. They were the people who were driving events. So when I first arrived there, the HVO were very confident and the BiH felt a little under pressure. But by the time I left, it was reversed, in that the HVO were not confident at all and the BiH were extremely confident and capable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to when, if you can tell us, as to when this change took place.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's that not an easy judgement to take, because it happened over a period of time. But I would say it was precipitated by Ahmici, and then when the BiH effectively took control of the Travnik area - and I can't remember exactly which month that was off the top of my head - but when that happened, I felt that the balance of power had shifted, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, what sort of facts made you conclude that the ABiH became the dominant military force?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The facts that enabled me to come to that conclusion was that they moved a number of brigades out of the Zenica area in order to conduct offensive operations, and those offensive operations took place in the Travnik area, and that was combined also with activity later on down near Gornji Vakuf. The result of that -- so what I'm saying, effectively, is the BiH turned their attention to gaining more territory and expelling, if you like, the HVO from that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, can the witness please be provided with a copy of Prosecution Exhibit P225. Prosecution Exhibit P225 is the milinfosum of 8 June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, if I may please draw your attention to the first page of this milinfosum and to the portion under "2," where it says: "The expected BiH offensive in the area has begun." And then the villages of Guca Gora, Brajkovici, Bukovica, Radonjici, and Maljine are mentioned. And then it is said that such forces "have been captured by the BiH." This statement in the milinfosum, is it a reflection of what you just described, that the ABiH became the more dominant force within ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is entirely correct. These advances and capturing of various towns and villages is the tangible evidence of that change.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And, of course, I understand, General, that this is a milinfosum that was produced by BritBat whilst you were in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's entirely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the exhibit please be removed from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, how would you describe the military equipment, or what do you think -- which army, which force was the stronger force, in terms of military equipment?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I would prefer, if I may, to answer that in a more rounded way and not just go for military equipment. What I'd like to go is -- describe is the capability of each force. They were very different. In my opinion, the HVO had less soldiers but they had more sophisticated equipment, in terms of artillery and -- a large artillery capability. They also, certainly further south, had access to HV artillery from Croatia to back up their fire power. On the other hand, the BiH had an awful lot more soldiers and they were, if you like, a people-heavy army, but they had very little artillery at all. But they did have a number of 120-millimetre mortars. So in terms of equipment, I think the HVO were less equipped but they had less soldiers and the BiH were not so well equipped but they had more soldiers. In terms of morale, which is a very important factor, I thought the BiH were much more determined than the HVO, and also in some cases better trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, you were just saying that the HVO 3rd Corps had more soldiers. Would it be fair to say that the ABiH 3rd Corps significantly outnumbered the HVO, in terms of manpower?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: In the Lasva Valley area, sir, I would say that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If we talk about the Lasva Valley area, does this include, in your view, also the area of Travnik and Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it would. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were headquartered in Vitez, did you get to know whether Muslim refugees arrived in the area of 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I did, because on a number of occasions we deployed to the Travnik and Turbe area, to the west of the Lasva Valley, and we set up the conditions to enable refugees who had been expelled - some from the Banja Luka area, Muslims, and they came across front lines. There were a considerable number of refugee centres in Travnik, and I was aware that people were coming in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Amongst the refugees, were there men of military age?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was considered being of military age?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I think "of military age," it's difficult to put exact dates on, but if you could -- if you were fit and you could carry a rifle and provisions and you were motivated, then you were of military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very well. Were Muslim refugees who were of military age, were they to your knowledge incorporated in ABiH 3rd Corps military units?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I believe they were. And in particular, I think, if my memory serves me correctly, the Krajina Brigade in Travnik had a number of people who had been expelled from the Krajina and specifically formed with their friends to form a brigade there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: From a military perspective, does it make sense to incorporate refugees in military units?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: To incorporate refugees who have been expelled from their homes and had their families killed in some cases I think was entirely legitimate and reasonable. It formed a strong, well-motivated fighting force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, what is your impression about the professionalism of ABiH 3rd Corps? And at this point in time I'm only talking about the issue whether you got to know whether the ABiH 3rd Corps had incorporated former JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I was aware there was a number of former JNA officers within the 3rd Corps. They were sort of sprinkled around all the way through. I knew that a number of 3rd Corps soldiers, as with the HVO soldiers, had done military service of a few weeks or even a few months. So there was considerable expertise within that corps, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What impact, if any, did the considerable expertise of the former JNA officers within ABiH 3rd Corps have on the discipline within the ABiH 3rd Corps units?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I think the 3rd Corps genuinely wanted to form an army which had the highest possible standards, and clearly, if you looked at them, their equipment was poor, their uniforms were scruffy. But that's not important in an army. What was important was that they were organised and trained. And everywhere I went I saw people organised and trained. I know they produced a certain amount of documents to help their soldiers. Indeed, they produced a little soldier's booklet, which helped, again, with the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's move on, General, to the next item, to the next subject I would like to cover with you, namely the so-called operational tempo. How would you describe, General, the operational tempo within the area of responsibility of ABiH 3rd Corps during the period you were deployed in Central Bosnia, meaning from May 1993 to November 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Operational tempo would normally be used as a term to describe the pace of activity of a military organisation. Within the BiH during that period, they would plan, I believe, very carefully, and they would take a move or a bite forward, if you like. They would then consolidate and plan for the next phase. They had to do this because they didn't have particularly good resupply systems. So it was a question of attack, move, and then pause; consolidate what you have, consider the next move, which would probably be already planned in the greater scheme; and then attack, move. So you get periods of intense activity interspersed by really quite quiet periods when the front lines are very quiet. It's a question of violent activity which gets you your success, and then you pause and hold and make sure it's consolidated before you move on. No commander would rush into a continuous movement, because he would soon run out of logistics and resupplies. So it was a measured tempo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The pauses and breaks you were just mentioning, were they a repeated occurrence in between the different military actions?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was the normal between each military action. It gave people time to recuperate, to refresh, to get new soldiers forward if required, for the wounded to be sorted out. It just -- and everything to be planned for the next phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Such repeated pauses and breaks in between military operations, were they often and long enough to allow the 3rd Corps commander, General Hadzihasanovic, to deal with disciplinary matters, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I would think he had time to do that. It would be one of -- I mean, in any army, one of the things you would wish to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And were these repeated operational breaks and pauses often and long enough to allow the 3rd Corps commander, General Hadzihasanovic, to fulfil his legal obligations to initiate steps to investigate and to follow up investigations in respect to allegations of crimes, including war crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I would estimate there would be sufficient time for that, on the basis that the action time is quite small, compared with, if you like, recuperation time. You do your violent actions, which may last one or two or three days, and then there would be a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, let's move on to the next issue, namely your direct contact with General Hadzihasanovic. Did you have direct contact with General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I met him before I took over as the BritBat commander, and then on a number of occasions throughout the six months. It was a personal meeting with my aides as well, normally in his headquarters in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were saying you had meetings on a number of occasions. For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you please be a bit more concrete. Do you have still a rough guess as to how often you met General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Probably about 18 to 20 times during those six months. So if you like, an average of per month is about three or so. It would depend on events. If I was away or if he was away, we wouldn't meet. But I tried to meet at regular intervals because it was important to keep that relationship going.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was General Hadzihasanovic your main contact within ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, he was. I mean, as the commanding officer, my main contact was with the senior BiH officer and the senior HVO officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already mentioned, General, that the meetings regularly took place in the ABiH 3rd Corps headquarters in Zenica. Who was actually the one who requested the meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It was a shared business. I often requested and occasionally Colonel Hadzihasanovic requested a meeting as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was discussed in the course of such meetings? What was the purpose of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The purpose of the meetings was for me to discuss with Colonel Hadzihasanovic what was going on, and we discussed politics in broad terms, the political situation, and then perhaps in more detail what was going on on the military side, both from the HVO point of view and the BiH. We then discussed any problems that might occur to do with the capture of prisoners, prisoner exchanges, problem areas, routes which we couldn't go along because they were blocked and I needed them to deliver the aid. All sort of -- not routine business, but it was business where I'd like a solution or we could move forward on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I think you already mentioned it. Did you take somebody with you when meeting Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I would take routinely Warrant Officer Burton, who was my bodyguard, and also - particularly with Hadzihasanovic - the captain who was assigned to him, and my military information officer, Captain Simon Harrison, who I mentioned previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And who was the captain who was assigned to Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It was originally Captain Cameron Kiggell for the first half of the tour, and then he was replaced by Captain Andrew Jackson for the second half of the tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whenever you had meetings, the 18 to 20 meetings within your six-month tour in Central Bosnia, were there any time limits, was there any pressure in terms of time when you had such meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. The meeting went on for as long as we both felt it was suitable. And when we'd run out of topics, we would then break up and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were already mentioning, General, that a liaison officer was assigned to Hadzihasanovic. Did there come a time when there were any problems with the liaison officer, in the sense that Hadzihasanovic was not happy with the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I think initially he thought it was very useful to have a direct link with the British Battalion through a liaison officer. As time went on and he also realised I had liaison officers in the various locations and brigades of the area, he was less happy because he realised we were getting the full picture of what his army was doing. And at one stage he requested that I removed the liaison officers from those brigades, which I did; but I then reassigned them to come back into areas, as opposed to brigades. And I must say there was a slight cat-and-mouse business we played, in me wanting to get information from my liaison officers and him quite frankly, and quite understandably, not wanting to give me perhaps all the information I needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: But do I understand you correctly, General, that playing this little cat-and-mouse game after you changed the assignment, you still received the very same amount of reliable information as prior to the change of assignments?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the JNA background of Hadzihasanovic, if any?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I knew him to be a former officer of the JNA. I believe he was a colonel. Apart from that, I didn't have -- no specific knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Having met him between 18 to 20 times and having been in the area for six months, General, what is your and what was your impression at the time about the competence of Hadzihasanovic, his military abilities, and the control of his troops within the ABiH 3rd Corps area?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: My assessment of Hadzihasanovic as an officer was that he was an extremely intelligent and capable commander. He had his headquarters in Zenica particularly well organised, with a number of functions to enable it to command. He had the communications and the staff, and that was his initiative, because he was the commander. He was very cool and calm. He was a thinker. He was not given to taking action without considering all the consequences. I had a huge respect for him as a commander. One criteria we use -- or criterion, rather -- we use in the British Army is whether somebody is at peace with himself as a commander. He knows where he wants to go and what he's got to do. And I would say that Colonel Hadzihasanovic was entirely that. He was a very, very proficient and capable officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Colonel Hadzihasanovic at the time, was he in your assessment and in your views, in full control of his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Very much so. I think he was in complete control of his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did he ever appear to be stressed?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No, he never appeared to be stressed. He was particularly calm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: During your time in Central Bosnia, did you also meet the counterpart of Colonel Hadzihasanovic at the time, namely Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And in a similar fashion to speaking to Colonel Hadzihasanovic, I would speak on the same matters to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And how would you describe the differences, if any, between Hadzihasanovic and Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic always gave me the impression of being a hunted man, as it were. He was quite nervous about things. He was a competent officer but not a brilliant officer. He was capable of doing his various tasks and commanding his area in not a very dynamic way, but he was a capable officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In terms of being calm and at peace with himself, was there a difference in comparison to Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, there was. And as events of the six months unfolded, he became more and more -- Blaskic became more and more perturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Talking about Hadzihasanovic again, was Commander Hadzihasanovic, to your knowledge, was he aware what was on -- what was going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I think he had a very effective machinery for gathering information and the communications to go with it. He was always, when I visited, very much up to date with what was going on on the ground and things that we discussed. If I opened a new line of thought, he would generally say, "I know about that, yes," and agree or disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This answer, General, implies that Hadzihasanovic was informed to the very detail you would expect a corps commander to be informed.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's exactly what I would expect, and he certainly was well informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, you already touched briefly on the next issue I wish to discuss with you. Did Hadzihasanovic, at the time you've been in Central Bosnia, did he have at his disposal the necessary staff to effectively command and control ABiH 3rd Corps, such as planning staff, administrative staff, military police, and communication abilities?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He had, as I mentioned before, a very effective headquarters, which covered the planning functions; he had a very able deputy, in the shape of Colonel Merdan, Dzemal Merdan, who was his second-in-command; he had administrative staff, and I often saw military police dressed with their white bandoliers and white boot covers on the streets and also at checkpoints; he had the equipment for communications. And if I could run through that, because I think it's quite important, for a corps commander. We had his satellite telephone number and a fax number as well, so we could communicate directly. In addition, he had a system of Motorola, a VHF radio, a hand-held radio, which he commanded his troops with. And initially we had telephones, but unfortunately as events unfolded, after the first month they were cut off. But I was quite clear that it was a good system of communication, including the ability to talk to Sarajevo and also to talk to his troops. And, for example, when some helicopters landed in Novi Travnik, that information got back to him very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, you were just describing the effective and efficient communication equipment and communication abilities within 3rd Corps, and in particular, the ones Hadzihasanovic had at his disposal. And one item were obviously satellite phones. And you are mentioning faxes as well. Was this a satellite fax?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: This was a satellite fax, yes. We had the telephone number to speak at voice, and also the fax number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Had you ever been provided with the satellite phone and satellite fax numbers?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, we were. We were given this is them directly. It wasn't withheld at all. And perhaps I should add, just to complete the picture, I also knew there were a number of ex-JNA radio trucks available, and we saw them from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The satellite phone and satellite fax numbers, do you still recall as to who provided you with the numbers and as to when you were provided with the numbers?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: In all honesty, I cannot remember when, but I know we had the numbers, because they're in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It's obviously some time ago, but was it more at the beginning of your tour or at the end of your tour?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It was at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The communication abilities and the communication equipment you just described in some detail, did such communication equipment and such communication abilities, did they meet the military standard at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The satellite phones were obviously very efficient. The ex-JNA VHF and HF communication, whilst they in Western terms were quite old, they were extremely efficient and reliable. The Motorolas - that is, the hand-held equipments - required repeaters up on the hills, and it was, I think, it was to everyone's advantage to leave those repeaters switched on. So both the HVO and the BiH used the same repeaters in the hills. It was a good system. It was the best available at the time. It wasn't perfect. No communication system is perfect. But it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, you just used a number of abbreviations. For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you please explain what these acronyms stand for, like VHF communication and so on.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do apologise. It was "very high frequency" and "high frequency" communications. Very high frequency would be used over a short range of something like 10 to 15 kilometres. But high frequency can be used either for short range or for hundreds of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General, for this clarification. That certainly helps a lot. Were these sophisticated means or the means of communications which met the military standards at the time, to your knowledge were they available to Hadzihasanovic throughout your time in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be provided with a copy -- or with Prosecution Exhibit P162.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: P162 is the milinfosum dated the 25th of June, 1993. General, if I may, please, draw your attention to page 3 of this milinfosum and to the portion under "4". The portion starts with: "CO 1 PWO." Can you please explain for the benefit of the Trial Chamber who is CO 1 PWO.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. CO 1 PWO is the acronym for the commanding officer of the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment Yorkshire, i.e., myself, the commander of BritBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The portion under "4" addresses a meeting you yourself had with commander 3rd Corps, Enver Hadzihasanovic, and it is making reference that he was in excellent spirits and that he "claimed that he had good comms with the area through a series of rebroadcast stations set on the hills." What does the abbreviation "comms" stand for, please?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It stands for "communications."

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What is written in this portion of the milinfosum, does it reflect the information -- the evidence you just provided the Trial Chamber with?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the exhibit please be removed from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These communication equipment and communication abilities, were they sufficient to enable Hadzihasanovic to gather all information he wanted to get and he needed to have as a corps commander?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I think they enabled him to gather -- it certainly enabled him to gather information as a corps commander. It wouldn't be the only way he gathered information. He would clearly have his own liaison officers working within his corps and the chain of command within the corps. But although they weren't the most perfect means of communication, I believe they worked very efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did these means of communication enable Hadzihasanovic to gather and to receive information in both directions, meaning within 3rd Corps and outside 3rd Corps, meaning information from other corps and information from the Supreme Command in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I think you earlier on mentioned that there were also portable communication equipment available. Can you please a bit elaborate on this one.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The portable equipment would be hand-held radios, which normally are a very short range, 2 or 3 miles. But if you have a repeater station on the hill, they will then boost the signal and enable it to go further. With a chain of repeater stations, you can actually communicate over quite long distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, General. The issue about communications we discussed in the context of the staff which Hadzihasanovic had at his disposal at the time. Let's come back to this issue in broader terms. General, was the quantity and the quality of staff at the disposal of Hadzihasanovic, was it sufficient to enable him to fully fulfil his duties as a corps commander?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I believe so. And the evidence for that I would take from my visits, when I found to -- my visits to Zenica, to 3 Corps - when I found industrious and capable staff officers, who invariably - even if the commander wasn't there - were able to brief me and tell me what was going on. And there was never ever problem with that. They were, to my mind - and it goes with Colonel Hadzihasanovic's character - he had assembled a very capable team. You had to be good to be in his corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your last answer, General, that you had to be good to be in his corps headquarters, does this answer imply that Colonel Hadzihasanovic at the time, that he was able to use his staff as good as possible?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. I think he had good staff. He was a natural leader. He was hugely respected by his headquarters staff and, actually, the staff in the various elements on the ground. He was a very effective and capable commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already mentioned the name earlier on, namely the name of Dzemal Merdan. Who was Dzemal Merdan at the time? What was his function and his duties?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I think -- I mean, I never had it described to me exactly, but I think he was the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps. I think his duties were to -- not only to deputise in the absence of Colonel Hadzihasanovic but also to look after things like communications, logistics, and all those bits and pieces that enable an army to work properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How close was Merdan to Hadzihasanovic and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Professionally, they were very close. I would say that in terms of command, that Hadzihasanovic was the dynamic commander, and Dzemal Merdan was the extremely loyal and capable second-in-command, who would fix things for his commander. Funnily enough, I don't think Dzemal Merdan would have made a good commander. He was the number two, he was the loyal number two that kept it going.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Also, you think, General, that Dzemal Merdan would not have made a good commander. What are your views in terms of his professionalism?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: He was a very experienced and professional officer. He certainly knew what to do and his jobs. When I say he wasn't a great commander, you're comparing with somebody who was very good. That's -- you know, this was a good team.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And you obviously are comparing Merdan with Hadzihasanovic, who was very good?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Dzemal Merdan, being the deputy of Hadzihasanovic, was he informed -- was he informed on what was going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, he was. If I'd -- on the odd occasion when I'd called in, if Hadzihasanovic wasn't there, then I'd get a full description of what was going on from Dzemal Merdan. He was also I know on a number of occasions would be dispatched out to deal with specific problems or to find out what was going on. So he was occasionally out in the field gathering information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Hadzihasanovic get to know what Merdan got to know, meaning did you get the impression that Merdan briefed Hadzihasanovic about everything he needed to know?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I got the impression that within the whole headquarters there was a very good system in 3rd Corps headquarters in making sure everybody knew what was going on, and that would include the relationship and the communication between Hadzihasanovic and Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, was there a certain nickname BritBat or others may have used for Colonel Hadzihasanovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I called him once "the cunning fox" because a fox is a very wily and very clever animal and very cunning, and I think that caught on within the British Battalion. I hope it didn't get out, but it might have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Obviously now it's out. In your view, was it the right nickname? And if so, why?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I think it was the right nickname. A fox works on his own; he know what is he wants to do; he's very clever, he's fit, he's active, he's doing things. And that was Hadzihasanovic; he was a very capable man.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, what did you get to know, if anything, about activities Colonel Hadzihasanovic at the time enjoyed during his leisure time? For example, were there times when he was visiting his family?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. There was an occasion when he went away and told me he was visiting his family. I think he went up north. I wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, be provided with Prosecution Exhibit P216.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, if I may please draw your attention to page 2 of this milinfosum dated the 18th of October, 1993 and to the portion under "4" small letter "b." Arabic "4" starts with: "CO 1 PWO," and I understand that's you yourself.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Under "b," there is written that Hadzihasanovic himself provided information in respect to his absence in Tuzla and that this absence had been a visit to his family. And there in brackets there is written "around 1 x week." What does it actually mean? Was it for a full week or was it once per week? Can you elaborate on this?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That would be for a full week, seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And in the portion which follows this statement, it says that Hadzihasanovic was seen visiting 2nd Corps. Did you get to know about this visit?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The reason it appears as a comment is because it is taken from the fact of another milinfosum or a report at some other date. But my OC A Company was based in Tuzla, in the north, where 2nd Corps were, and he had seen Colonel Hadzihasanovic up there in 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, did you get to know, since this visit was obviously in the second half of October 1993, about a combined 3rd Corps-2nd Corps operation in the area of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. If you put the facts together that we disassembled in the various milinfosums, it became apparent to me that there was some cooperation between 3rd and 2nd Corps, and I assumed that that was going to be military cooperation at some stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the exhibit please be removed from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, you just informed the Trial Chamber that Colonel Hadzihasanovic at the time had the free time to visit his family for a full week in October 1993. What else, if anything, General, did you get to know about any activities Hadzihasanovic enjoyed during his leisure time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: He invited me to a picnic on the banks of a river where his other officers -- his corps commanders were assembled, which was a very relaxed and present event in very cordial and relaxed. We had a full and delicious, beautifully prepared meal. We sat on the grass. The sun was shining. It was a very pleasant afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Obviously in a very relaxed atmosphere.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Very relaxed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is there anything else you got to know about activities or sports Hadzihasanovic enjoyed in his leisure times?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Well, actually, before I went on my rest and recuperation, which is a two-week period away from the operational theatre - I went home to Germany - I asked him whether he'd like me to bring anything back. And he asked if he could have a fishing reel, because I think he'd broken his fishing reel on his fishing rod, and I brought one back for him. So I assumed, because he wanted it, that he was quite a keen fisherman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I note it's 10.25. There's one further issue I would like to discuss with the general. I would suggest, if the Trial Chamber agrees, to cover this issue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Mr. Withopf. We shall make a break now at 10.25, and we shall resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, there's one last issue I wish to discuss with the general, and I anticipate that I won't need longer than 15 to 20 minutes at the very maximum. And the issue I'm going to discuss with General Duncan is the issue of Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, what did you get to know in respect to the Mujahedin? Did you get to know whether Mujahedin were operating within the 3rd Corps area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I had reports that the Mujahedin were operating within the 3rd Corps area of responsibility, but of all the information I got, information on the Mujahedin was probably the most difficult to prove, the most difficult to verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you in your commanding position as the BritBat commanding officer, you yourself did not come across a Mujahedin, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That is correct. I came across a number of what I call local Mujahedin, who were locals who dressed up and tried to make out they were Mujahedin, but not the proper thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Trial Chamber has certainly noted, Mr. President, that my colleague is leading the witness. It would perhaps be better to ask questions of an open kind so as to avoid leading the witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I certainly do acknowledge that was a leading question, and it was a deliberate leading question in order to shorten the examination of the witness. I will ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, did you yourself ever personally see a Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: On what basis is the information you will provide the Trial Chamber with about the Mujahedin? On what is it based?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Information is based on my information-gathering machinery, which enabled me to know what was going on throughout the area. And there were, during the time we were in BritBat, in those six months, a number of reports, many unconfirmed, that Mujahedin were operating within the 3 Corps area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What information did your information-gathering machinery provide you with in respect on how Mujahedin were used within the ABiH 3rd Corps area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The subject of how the Mujahedin were used by 3rd Corps was a subject that I discussed at length with Captain Simon Harrison, my military information officer, and also my second-in-command, Richard Watson. It was something that for us was not entirely clear, and it was something that we would sift through every ounce of information we had to try and find out what was going on. Some aspects of the Mujahedin I could not understand. What I couldn't understand was their business of being told that they were operating out of control. That was very often a comment which was picked up from the ground and from information that, these people were not under command of 3rd Corps. I found that very difficult to swallow because from a military sense, any commander has a limited number of assets which he can use, and if you are allowing somebody who's not under your command to consume ammunition, supplies and food, you are diverting your main effort. And therefore, I assumed that those Mujahedin must be under 3rd Corps command, because if they wasn't under the command -- or rather, if they weren't under the command, then they would be diverting assets from 3rd Corps. And this in military terms is something that a senior military officer would not is not the way to do business, and certainly when I teach and instruct on brigade and corps commander courses that we run, maintenance of a very clear focus and the maximum use of assets and not diverting your assets is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: General, did you ever discuss the issue of the Mujahedin with Hadzihasanovic and/or Merdan?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It came up on a number of occasions because I never really knew whether they existed or not. In many ways, I thought whether they existed or not somebody would need to invent them because in terms of a very effective weapons system, their presence was enormous. If people knew that Mujahedin were about to arrive, villages would be immediately evacuated. They had a massive effect. And I believe they were used as a very effective propaganda tool by 3rd Corps. It was something you could deny but actually encourage. And that was a very useful weapon system, because at the end of the day you win a battle by defeating people's minds, not their physical beings. And the Mujahedin were particularly good at that. It was an impressive, very careful, and carefully orchestrated use of them. You could deny at times; you could admit at times. But in terms of running a campaign, having those Mujahedin, whether they existed or not, was extremely useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly that the issue of Mujahedin was used as a propaganda tool; but do I also understand you correctly that Mujahedin were in the area of 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I believe they were both used as a propaganda tool and there were reports - although I personally didn't see them - from my people on the ground referring to the presence, just occasionally, of Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whenever you discussed the issue of Mujahedin operating within the 3rd Corps area of responsibility, either with Colonel Hadzihasanovic at the time or his deputy, Dzemal Merdan, what was their response in terms of commanding and controlling the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Nobody admitted to commanding and controlling them, but I do remember one occasion when Dzemo Merdan said he had instructed Mehmed Alagic to sort out the Mujahedin in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: With the permission of the Trial Chamber, can the witness please be provided with Defence Exhibit DH72.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: DH72 is the milinfosum dated the 14th of June, 1993. General, if I may please draw your attention to page 1 of this milinfosum, paragraph 1, towards the end of paragraph 1, towards the portion which reads: "When questioned about the activities of the Mujahedin, Merdan claimed that they were outside the effective control of 3rd Corps. Hadzihasanovic showed a letter he had written to his higher command seeking authority to deal with what he considered to be a problem." And reference is made at the very beginning of this portion again to CO 1 PWO, who is obviously you yourself. Do you recall, General, this conversation?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I do recall the conversation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And does what's written in this milinfosum, does it reflect the usual attitude and response of Hadzihasanovic and Merdan in respect to the issue of Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can this exhibit please be removed from the witness and can, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, the witness please be again provided with Prosecution Exhibit P216.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P216 is the milinfosum dated 18 October 1993. And if I may draw your attention, General, to page 2, paragraph 4. At the very end of paragraph 4 or at the end of paragraph 4, under "e," it says: "Questioned on the actions of Muslim extremists toward remaining Croat minorities in BiH controlled areas, Hadzihasanovic side-stepped the issue completely" and "did not acknowledge that there was a problem." Again, reference is made to CO 1 PWO, who is obviously you. Do you recall this meeting, this conversation with Colonel Hadzihasanovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And does this statement of Hadzihasanovic again reflect his attitude towards the problem of Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the exhibit please be removed from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you, General, at the time whilst you've been in Central Bosnia and do you believe today, do you believe the statements made by Hadzihasanovic and Merdan in respect to the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I do not. I believe that the Mujahedin were used as a very efficient propaganda system, as an efficient weapons system, which is easily deniable. And I think it was part of the campaign plan to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How would you judge, General, on the statement that they were out of control?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I don't think they were out of control. I think they were specifically tasked, in terms of the overall campaign plan that 3rd Corps had produced to be used, with great efficiency to speed up attacks and to cut the way forward. It is the planning and use of the Mujahedin, I think, was very carefully controlled. I thought at once they were controlled by Merdan; I can't prove that. But that was a feeling. I think they were controlled at the highest level by 3rd Corps as a very, very efficient means of doing business. The JNA as an army are very well trained in the art of deception and this sort of business, with deception and moving people and minds and getting influence like that, is very characteristic. It is also the characteristic of a very good commander and it doesn't surprise me that Hadzihasanovic would use them like that, because he's got that bigger picture of using whatever assets he can to get what he wants to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. I shall consequently give the floor to the Defence team. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning, General Duncan. Let me first introduce myself, because we did not have the opportunity of meeting before. I am present before you this morning with my colleague Mr. Alexis Demirdjian and my colleague, Mrs. Vedrana Residovic, and my name is Stephane Bourgon, counsel representing General Hadzihasanovic. General, I have, of course, my questions ready for you this morning, but I'd like first to begin by asking you a quick question: Coming here this morning, I thought that from a two-star general we would discuss something else than fishing reels who were bought for the son of your friend General Hadzihasanovic. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I never mentioned being bought for his son. I mentioned being bought for him. He was -- this is a very good commander. I wouldn't expect Hadzihasanovic to be rushing round. You know, you need your rest. It's one of the characteristic things. Commanders pace themselves very carefully. And you asked me whether we had quiet moments. Yeah, there were quiet moments when -- things happen very quickly in war and then stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And according to your story, we can come to two conclusions: The first conclusion, of course, is that everything was perfect. Two professional armies; one has weapons, one has manpower. They both have professional staffs. They both have the necessary communications. And they are involved in the war. And there's nothing more to it. Is that your opinion, General?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
