utterances.text: With the greatest respect, I regard that as a very naive statement. And I'm sorry I've said that, but I think this was an extremely complex business. Ethnic issues were involved. It was not simple. My position in the middle of this war was very unique. I was in somebody else's war, but not at war. And we were trying to get aid through at the same time. This was a complex, tricky, and difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So then it was not the best and -- the best of both armies and the best of worlds, was it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No, I haven't said that. I said that both armies had their limitations in kit and supplies on one side and in manpower on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Nevertheless, General, you will stick to your story, I imagine, about the efficiency, the intelligence, the planning, and the exercise of command by General Hadzihasanovic in the toughest of circumstances, would you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I would -- yes. He was a very capable commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the circumstances were indeed very difficult for any commander.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I may just quote you before I get to my first question. I'd like to quote you from a couple -- this is an article I have with me which you wrote in 1994, coming out of Bosnia. And I would like to quote you from this article. Would you agree with me that it is your impression that this six months was in fact for yourself the most unusual six months in all, your entire time spent in the British Army?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: To that date, yes. I have spent a very unusual six months since then in Sierra Leone with the United Nations, which was the most demanding thing I've ever done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me, General, that you once said that "There was no logic to this conflict, that a whole group of people could suddenly change their allegiance and would be fighting alongside another ethnic group and that even today in the north end of Tuzla" - now you're talking 1994 - "at the tip of the finger there are still Serbs fighting against Serbs and that the Muslims and the Croats throughout my tour in Bosnia and well after my battalion had left were very much at odds in Central Bosnia"? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, could I ask what the document is being quoted is exactly? I mean, you're saying I wrote this and said it. I'd like to know when and what, please. Is that all right, sir? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Maitre Bourgon, could you give us your reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I be helped by the Usher, please, because there's a whole series of documents that I shall be presenting in the course of my cross-examination, so that I can ask some of these documents to be tendered into evidence when I've finished. Some of these documents have already been tendered; others have not. At the end of my cross-examination, I shall ask some of these documents to be withdrawn and others to be tendered so that things are quite clear. I have three binders, Your Honour: One for the witness and all the documents can be made available to all the people present in the courtroom, including the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General. I'm informed that the tabs could not be put in time, so this is the before-last document in your binder. And this is a paper which you wrote in 1994 in some magazine called "Defence and International Security." Do you recall writing this paper, General?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would like to quote -- if you look at this paper, I would like to go to the third paragraph, and I will quote you as saying: "I will concentrate on two areas, the first being the British Battalion and its tasks; how we did that task, our deployment"; and then after that I will pick up on some themes: "from what for me was a most unusual six months, perhaps the most unusual six months of my entire time in the British Army." So we went over this one already, and you agreed with me that this was your thought.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I move, General, to the last paragraph on this first page, six lines from the bottom, where you say that: "On reflection back in my battalion's base in Germany, I realised that Bosnia was a very unique area and the task equally unique. There was no template to be drawn from my experiences in the army and the easy solution of -- 'if it has worked somewhere else, so it will work here' was clearly a non-starter. It wasn't a task the British Army had done before. It was unusual to be in a war but not at war. We were effectively sitting right in the middle of somebody else's civil war." Is that your statement, General?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. And that refers to the position obviously of myself and my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can move to the second page. And I'll finish with this document so then we can move on. I would like to move to page -- sorry, if you look at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: There are page numbers, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is the page where we speak about normality in Bosnia, and there's no -- to page 17. And page 17 on the right side, General, where it says: "Normality in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then you say: "I would just like to finish with some comments on a number of areas. The first one is the effect of living on the front line." And you say: "Both Vitez and Gornji Vakuf were effectively in no man's land for between four and six months, so it does become a little bit of a problem. Everyone was shot at, shelled, or mined at some stage. Normally in the army everything is reported very calmly. But in Bosnia there was so much fighting we had to be a bit selective." If we move down to the last page of this document --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Could I make an observation before we move?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely, General.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: You've just read out a section which refers to the way we reported things. What you didn't read out is the lines below that. What I was referring to there is if we were fired at generally and bullets were not coming near us, that was quite normal and we didn't report it. What we did report was the serious attacks that were life-threatening or wounding. And the selection, therefore, is nothing to do with general business; it's just specifically concerned with reporting incidents that happened to us while we were in there for six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So am I to understand from this comment, General, that the incidents that are reported in the milinfosums are all serious incidents that are above what you've just described?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Milinfosums are there to record major events and as much as possible as we can put down. In terms of length, you have to be as concise as possible in your speech when you do a milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you had to write everything that happened to you in the milinfosums, it would take many more pages; would that be true, General?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That would be true, but that was one of the purposes of the meeting at 1800 hours, to make sure people understood the background and the situation to what was in the milinfosums.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me move on, General, to some of the questions I have for you this morning. But as a preliminary, I'd like to confirm that you've testified as a Prosecution witness in both the Blaskic and the Kordic cases.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that the basis for this testimony was a statement that you provided to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor, and that was in August of 1996 and April of 1997. Do you recall meeting the investigators on both of these occasions?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I do recall meeting investigators, and I recall having made two statements prior to the one that we've used already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in May of 2000, General, you were requested to provide a further statement focussing more specifically on the events related to this case.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And yesterday, General, you met with the Prosecution to prepare for your testimony today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at the time you met with the Prosecution, you were asked whether you were willing to meet with counsel for the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic and General Kubura, and you refused.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: May I ask why you refused to meet Defence counsel, General?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: As I recall, I had not met the Defence counsel on the previous two court cases, and I decided I didn't wish to meet with the Defence counsel in this case. It's a personal decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what is that personal decision based on, General?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It's based on the fact that I was appearing here and had been asked to appear here as a witness for the Prosecution, and that's what I was going to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So as such, you are biased and you have taken already the side of the Prosecution and you come here not to give facts but, as a matter of fact, to testify against General Hadzihasanovic; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I find that comment unusual from somebody in your position, which implies that an officer from the British Army, who specialises in ethics apart from anything else, would deliberately come here to lie and cheat and et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I take it, General, that you believe in the rule of law and the presumption of innocence, do you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in that article that we just reviewed, I refer your attention to page 12. In page 12, at the bottom on the left side, where it says "Local commanders," it says at the end, five lines from the bottom: "On one occasion, we received a phone call in the base at half past 8.00 in the morning, and I was not there. Enver Hadzihasanovic, the commander of 3rd Corps, would not leave a message. When I saw him the next day, I asked him for what the phone call was about. He just said 'I had promised you to ring you before we attacked and I like to keep my promises.'" This, General; you recall this event?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also recall, General, a similar event where on one occasion General Hadzihasanovic told you, "Are you not seeing my counterpart today," to which your answer was yes? Do you recall this event?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that particularly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, then we'll read a little further down in this text. And I'd like to quote you where you talk about the chess match that is going on between you and General Hadzihasanovic. And I quote you on the right side of page 12, in the middle of the page, where it says: "'Do you see my opposite number? I said 'of course I do. I'm seeing him this afternoon'. He said 'what time?' 'about 4.00.' 'Where?' 'Hotel Vitez." He then said" -- we're talking about General Hadzihasanovic -- at least, it is my understanding -- "'okay, make sure you are out by half past 5.00.'" And you were not out at half past 5.00, you left at 25 minutes to 6.00. And at that time the shelling of the hotel began. You can leave the document aside. Did General Hadzihasanovic actually inform you of this attack on Hotel Vitez, which as we both know, was the headquarters of General Blaskic? Is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: He didn't inform me he was going to attack it. He just asked me to be out by a certain time, which I failed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And from your previous conversation, where he had promised to inform you, if I take it from this text, you took this as being a warning or did you disregard it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I left late.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did the attack begin while you were still there?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it did. And I certainly wouldn't volunteer to be shelled, as I'm sure you're aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, you said all these nice things about General Hadzihasanovic. And this man on two occasions as a minimum informed you of incoming or intended operations by the ABiH in order to facilitate your job, did he not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: He informed me on many occasions of -- of forthcoming operations by the BiH, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you understand that he had no obligations whatsoever to inform you of such attack, did he?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No. I merely asked him and we agreed and we had an agreement on that particular subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when your battalion deployed out of the area sometime in November, did you not have a conversation at which time General Hadzihasanovic assured you that he would do his utmost to ensure that you would have an easy way out with your battalion? Do you recall this moment?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I don't particularly recall that moment, but I do remember that Mehmed Alagic made some promise to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, General, we'll quote again from -- if you just read that text. And it's on the same page, at the bottom of that same paragraph, just above. And you say on this paragraph: "Despite -- we were actually very good friends." And then you say: "In another incident before the end of my time in Bosnia, he said to me, 'When are you leaving with your troops?' I replied I would be out on 15 November and added that it would be nice to have a peaceful time to move out because the move is quite complicated. Hadzihasanovic laughed and added in turn, 'We entirely understand and we will not attack or intimidate any British/UN soldiers until the 16th, and then we'll give hail to the incoming battalion.'" Is that -- do you recall this conversation?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I do recall it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I recall, in your Blaskic statement that you provided when you testified, you said that this was Alagic who had done this. So who is it? Are we supposed to take this article that you write in a magazine or are we supposed to take what you say in a court of law?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: You would have to make your decision on that. I can't remember exactly. I mean, I've written it down here. I believed it was Alagic or Hadzihasanovic. I can't exactly say which. What I can say is that certainly a senior commander agreed from the BiH that that's what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, if I ask you for your personal opinion, a man such as General Hadzihasanovic, with whom you've had many relationships during six months, a man who tried to make your job easier, a man who warned you of his attacks, a man who went beyond the call of duty to facilitate your work; wouldn't you agree with me that a man like that, General, deserves at least that you will agree to meet his Defence counsel to facilitate your testimony before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I don't think there's a linkage between the two, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, General, I'd like to know if prior to coming here, if you've had any discussions with your former officers. And I will specifically name three names, Major Kent-Payne.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I haven't spoken to Major Kent-Payne for a number of years, since he was asked to resign from my regiment and move to another regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about Major Bower?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I haven't spoken to Major Bower for possibly two or three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about Mr. Cameron Kiggell, who has left the service?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I haven't spoken to him since he left the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, prior to your deployment, it is my understanding based on what you said in the Blaskic case that you had been in command of your battalion for some 30 months.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I take it from that that you knew the officers well and that you trusted them and that they trusted you.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That would be a fair statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that this is a very important basis which is necessary for effective command and control?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that if, as you say, General Hadzihasanovic had a solid headquarters, there must have been some kind of similar relationship between him and his subordinates and his subordinates towards him?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In your statement, you mention that you were informed about your deployment to Bosnia in 1993 as part of Operation Grapple 2. Is that --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I was informed officially in 1993. I was warned unofficially, which was not recorded, in 1992 that I'd be going.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because I myself was surprised that you would only be informed in 1993 because of the necessity to prepare for your battalion and because the next rotation, at least in my limited knowledge of the military, is usually informed before the first one actually deploys. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It is a fair statement, yes. And I was aware when the Cheshire Battalion deployed that we would be deploying after them, although I was not allowed to broadcast that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you did train your battalion before deploying, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And such training included individual training, collective training, as well as mission-specific training, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that such training is not only common practice within professional armies, such as that of the United Kingdom, but that it is also an absolute necessity directly linked to the success of a military mission?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, would you also agree that for an army, an army formation, let's say the size of a corps, that to be thrown in combat - that is, in real combat as you saw it in Bosnia - without having had the opportunity to train, would you agree that this would have serious consequences on the accomplishment of the mission and that it would impose a heavy burden on the chain of command as a whole but even more so on the commanding general of such formation?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: If you're comparing a British Army unit with a Bosnian army unit, I thinks that a comparison you can't make. There is a difference between apples and pears. We were trained specifically for that task and spent a lot of time preparing for that task. Based on our experience of counterinsurgency operations in the past in Malaya and considerable experience from Northern Ireland. I was a force moving into that theatre. You're comparing me with a force that's already in theatre. I don't think it's a like comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, if I take this forces that in theatre but that is throw in combat without having had the opportunity to train, would that be a serious impediment to the accomplishment of the mission?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It depends entirely on -- I mean, the training of a force is but one element of preparation, and you know that I think as well as I do. The motivation of a force is a very important element. And the BiH, as I think I've already said this morning, were a hugely well-motivated force. And I believe they had a very good command structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, you are in charge or responsible for the training of all the land army in the UK.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm asking you to concentrate and to focus on one criteria, which is training, and I'm asking you a very specific question: If an untrained army is thrown into combat, does that make it difficult for this army?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It makes it initially quite difficult. But if you are thrown into combat, you learn very quickly. And I can tell you one example: From the British Army, we arrived in Vitez and up until then we had been driving around in our armoured vehicles with quite a lot of our body and head exposed. After you get fired a lot at, you realise to keep your head down. You learn very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is exactly what one of your officers said before this Tribunal, when he said that you did not agree with the posture adopted by your predecessor, Colonel Stewart, whom you thought was too aggressive when you landed in Bosnia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I have not heard that comment from that particular officer. Every commanding officer in the British Army will command in the way that he thinks appropriate. I organised myself command to deal with the situation I found in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that is why, General, if you take two commanders at whatever level and the two may command in a different manner and yet both be very effective; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I would agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if the training or the lack of training makes it more difficult - we've agreed on that - does it also make the job, the work of the commanding general more difficult?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It is one task he will have to turn his eye to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Amongst many other tasks, of course.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Amongst many other tasks. And commanders are busy but commanders have staff and commanders issue directives.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, if under such circumstances the commanding general takes the necessary steps to train his troops, despite the adverse condition - you've described yourself the adverse conditions - would this illustrate to you that this commander is placing an emphasis on the accomplishment of his mission?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Naturally it would, yes, if he's trying to get his mission achieved and he requires extra training to achieve it, then that will be part of his plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would you also agree with me, General, that this such training is also a powerful measure towards the prevention of crimes or of violation of discipline by untrained troops?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It would help, yes, if the training has been effective, if the training has covered everybody it should do, and if the rules and regulations are published to back up that training.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. As for yourself, you found it necessary, as you've explained, before deploying to Bosnia and Herzegovina to conduct two detailed recces in early February and then again in early March; is that --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It was important for you --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Sorry, it was late January and early February. We deployed in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have the exact dates here in your statement, which says from 30 January until 6 February and then again from the end of February to, I guess, the 6th of March. But I'm not here to argue on dates.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I think -- sir, could I just clarify this? I did two reconnaissances each week and then deployed early, on the 6th of Marc h, took over on the 11th. That is quite important because the time spent on those reconnaissances was for me hugely important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's exactly my point, General. It was important for you to familiarise yourself with the area, to get an understanding of the conditions on the ground, and to prepare to accomplish the mandate given to you by the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. Because I was moving into the area, into an area which I hadn't been in before. Those forces that were deployed in the area had lived and grown up with the situation, so they were hugely aware of what was going on. As an outsider, I needed to spend a lot of time, hence my two reconnaissances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you would agree with me therefore that getting to know not only the area but also the military forces in this area was paramount to the success of your mission?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this is important because of course the conditions, the situation, and the circumstances in which these forces operate have a direct bearing on the exercise of command by the commanders you would be dealing with on the ground.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Could you repeat that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I'm not entirely clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will split the question into two.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I can't quite fathom the point you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the conditions, the situation, and the circumstances in which the forces operate on the ground have a direct bearing on the exercise of command by their commanders?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. But I would add that command goes with a number of principles which you do, and nothing is templated. You would therefore apply those principles to the conditions, situations and circumstances you find. But command as a function doesn't change. It is there. You are the commander. You exercise command. You adjust your methods; your keep your principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And for you, General, the fact that if you could familiarise yourself with the conditions, the situation, and the circumstances, you would also be in a better position to understand the counterparts you would be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I agree. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it would have also been important for you and for the accomplishment of your mission to know and understand the role, the modus operandi of the other players present on the ground, namely the ECMM, the ICRC, the UNHCR, and maybe other NGOs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That is correct. And I visited all those agencies on my reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I take a look at the law applicable, the law of the land, would that also be something that would be important to understand in order to deal with your counterparts in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It was important that I understood entirely military law; British law as it applies, because that applies to a soldier wherever they are; and I was not aware of some of the laws of the land, because that -- in preparation for coming to Bosnia or deploying to Bosnia, that was an area I did not touch, the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And is it an area that it was important for you to consider when dealing with the military commanders on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. And I've recognised that in hindsight, because I now have in my organisation for training a bunch of lawyers who are particularly engaged in operational law. At that time, we hadn't done a deployment like this before. It was totally unique. If I had to go back and do it again, I would have probably taken a lawyer with me on day one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And now, General, today you are testifying - and you are testifying against General Hadzihasanovic on behalf of the Prosecution - and I put it to you that you still don't know what the legal regime applicable was in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you don't know what the platform of the government was and what instructions General Hadzihasanovic was receiving from his government.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I was the military officer sent to Bosnia to complete a military task. There was a civil affairs officer who was deployed with me, and there was a civil affairs set-up that dealt with what I call "the political side of things." My task was to get that aid through to people, people under command of the HVO and people under command of the BiH. That was my primary task. I think we were successful in that task and I took the measures and trained my troops in order to make sure we had success in that task. It was a unique task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was referring to, General. I wanted to ensure that we both understood that your mission remained a military mission and that all these civil matters that were taking place in Bosnia, you did not pay attention to because it wasn't your area of responsibility. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It's not correct I say I didn't pay attention to them. I was aware of them. But in terms of apportionment of my tasks and time, it was not as important as commanding my troops, which was my first responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, in your statement, you mention that during all your time in Bosnia you did not meet with civil authorities other than for once when you met with the mayor of Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I met with -- yeah, I met with the major of Zenica -- Zenica, pardon. I also met on occasions by chance with some of the officials from Vitez .

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is that the time when those rumours about offering you money for weapons was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's one of the occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this is -- you mentioned this in your article that you wrote, but you also referred to that in your statement. Please correct me if I'm wrong, but you were at that time sitting in a meeting with officials from the Zenica Municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at some point this gentleman decided that he needed to speak to you one on one.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And he had everyone leave the room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at that time, he said, "You seem to understand the situation of Muslims. What about if I offer you 2 million to get some weapons in Central Bosnia." Did he ask you that question?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: He did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when he answered -- your answer was, "2 million is not enough," at which point he left the room and went to see his counterpart into another room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That is correct, but I would add that it was just so surreal for me because I'd never been off the record a bribe like that before and my reaction was that wasn't enough. I didn't think they could possibly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And by leaving him leave that room, did you not imply that you were ready to take such a bribe?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: If I'd given that impression at the time, it was wrong. I hadn't consciously given that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I move on, General --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Could I -- could I add that when he came back -- could you just follow that through and when he came back I said, "I'm sorry, a British officer would never take a bribe." I made that quite clear to him at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have no doubt about that, General. If I move on to the fact of the legal situation in which General Hadzihasanovic was operating. We mentioned instructions he might have received from his government. But we should also mention the legal regime in terms of the fact that in Zenica at the time the local government was still operating, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that there was a sharing of responsibilities between General Hadzihasanovic, as commander of the 3rd Corps, and what was going on in town. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I would agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I mention to you that it was the civil police who was responsible for any civil disturbance or from any common-law crimes in town, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I would agree that was possibly the case, but I don't know under what status in Zenica martial law prevailed, because there were an awful lot of military police on the ground as well, both in the city and in the surrounding area. And they were not -- I don't know if they were in the jurisdiction of the civil or the military side. I assumed the military side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't know --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: This was a nation of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, you didn't feel it was required for you, as the senior military figure on the ground, to understand this relationship before you could testify against General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It's not a question of my understanding the relationship. I was aware that there were military police on the ground and civilian police. I would be very interested to know what that relationship between those two things -- people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And at the time, you did not feel it was necessary to -- to learn what this relationship was so you could understand the counterpart you were dealing with.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I understood from the presence of military police that they had some influence in keeping the situation under control. I would be very interested to know if there was an agreement between civil and military police or who was in control. If you could tell me that, that would be quite helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's move on to your own mission as UNPROFOR as commander of BritBat, which was, as you just stated a few minutes ago, to escort humanitarian convoys from UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No. I gave the task as to create the conditions whereby aid could be delivered into and through my area of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, that was your interpretation --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- of the mission you were given; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your mission was to escort --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, whose mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your mission?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That was part of my mission, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please pause between question and answer for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Was it your mission to escort humanitarian convoys from UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It was. And I was given the discretion which I discussed with General Morillon as to how I would achieve that. When you are given a mission by commander, you will go straight back to him and discuss to make sure he is entirely happy with what you are doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, General, the -- I'm informed that I need to slow down and that we need to pause between our questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I will endeavour to --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I will indeed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- to slow down. Now, of course, you know that your mission was authorised pursuant to Chapter 6 of the United Nations Charter.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, of course, you know the difference between a mission authorised under Chapter 6 and a mission authorised under Chapter 7 of the United Nations Charter. You understand the difference?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yeah. In broad terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you understand, General, that under Chapter 6 of the United Nations Charter there are three conditions for a peacekeeping mission. Do you recall these three conditions?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I don't -- I have to admit that I don't off the top of my head, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If I suggest to you that as follows: One, the consent of the parties; two, that you are to focus on your mission without interfering with the warring factions or in any other words to conduct your operations with impartiality; and three, that you are limited in terms of the force which you can use to self-defence. Would those be the three conditions of a normal peacekeeping mission?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I don't know. And I'll have to take it that you have taken them correctly from the Chapter 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you give those courses to the battalion commanders that you were referring to, is that not a topic that you cover?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Sorry, what isn't?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You mentioned a little earlier that you give training to battalion commanders and senior officers. Is that not a topic you cover?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It is a topic that I cover, and what is very important is to translate UN mandates and missions into fact on the ground. That is very important. And I'll give you an example. At one stage I was asked by the UN to monitor a convoy. What does that mean? Does it mean to protect it? Does it mean to guard it? Does it make sure nobody is killed, does it help it along, take some stuff off it. You have to interpret things applicable to the ground. And that is what we did. That is why I changed the mission of my battalion in agreement with General Morillon, my commander, to be that creating the conditions. And you will agrees that a slight change to the original mission given. But my commander at the time, General Morillon, was entirely happy with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, to put it another way, where you were in Bosnia, would you agree with me that this was not your war and unless you were attacked you were not authorised to use force, despite the superiority of your equipment such as, for example, the Warriors you were driving in?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. I would agree with that, and you may or may not be aware, but my Warrior is equipped with machine-guns and a cannon. And throughout that tour, despite all that happened, we never fired that cannon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you mentioned in this paper that nevertheless - and you regret doing so - that you did kill quite a number of people.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. And every single case where people were killed has been documented by the military police. And all witnesses to that event have been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you talk about those Warriors, you would agree with me that this is a powerful combat vehicle which imposes respect by its mere presence, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That why I was spent with those vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'm looking at this, again, your article, where it says -- I'm looking at the exact place where you talk about the Warriors and the use of force. And you mention in there that you considered yourself to be, whether you like it or not, the most powerful man in the land.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. But having the power is important; using it is a very different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, notwithstanding your limited mission, General, officers of your battalion have explained before this Chamber that you had the views - and this is reflected also in that paper - that your mandate was creating the necessary conditions for the delivery of humanitarian assistance, and that included for you close liaison with the parties and getting the information related to their operations which could impact on the convoys passing through Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in this article - I just used what they put into square brackets - on page 12, where it says: "I believe that if we knew exactly what was happening in every last square inch of our area, then we will hold an element of power." Those are your words.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. I can't see it on the page, but I take it you've read it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Page 12 in the big square.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you. Yes. That has been taken by the -- that is taken by the editor of that page. I did not put that in as it stands there. It is taken to enhance or de-hance the script, by the -- I mean, I have proved the script. The way it's been laid out there is an editorial trick which you are well used to of taking a sentence out and putting it in a little page in order to create impact. It's taking it out of context, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, actually, it's quoted straight into the paper, But I have limited time, so let's on --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No, hang on. I'd like to be quite clear on this. The little box in the middle which has a sentence is part of another bit of the script, is it not, and you've taken it out and said -- and stated that as a statement on its own. And I would suggest to you that an incorrect way of using it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will find the exact place where it is in the script and come back to that a little later. Now, you knew, General, that because this was a Chapter 6 mission and that you were supposed to be impartial; that you were not supposed to gather intelligence as you would do it if you were a party to this conflict. Did you know?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. And our intelligence-gathering was put under the concept of military information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that there's a big difference between intelligence-gathering and the type of military information you were collecting?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: There is -- the principles and the way we collect it would be very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what is the difference between the two? Would you agree with me that in the first case you need to know everything because you have to defend yourself and your life depends on it; and in the second case, where you collect military information, the idea is to know what's going on so that you can do your job.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Which is very different.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And even though you did not have the necessary resources to gather intelligence - you would agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I had fairly good resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You had human resources but not electronic resources, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No, I didn't have electronic resources, but I thought I had explained earlier on the system we had for gathering information, which given the resources I had I believed was the most efficient way to have doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So given the resources you had was the most efficient way.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But of course, if you had been in a war situation, the resources deployed for intelligence-gathering would have been much more significant.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Not necessarily. The American Army has deployed to Iraq and it is sadly missing human intelligence and resources at the bottom end being picked up from their soldiers. They have a big gap in their intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Nevertheless, General, you will agree with me that even the Americans in Iraq deploy with satellites, satellite imagery, radio interception, telephone interception.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Radar?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes and that's all things I didn't have access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That was my only point.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, even though you did not have the necessary resources that I've just mentioned, you did obtain some information by deploying the people you did, as you mentioned, and that your aim was to know what was happening for the next days of activities.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, even though it was standard operating procedure, or SOP as you may refer to this term, for BritBat personnel not to leave the compound at night -- is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It's a fair statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that of course impeded on your ability to observe the true story, because as you know, most troop deployments take place during the night and attacks are always launched before first light. So this, the fact that you were not --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Or last light.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Or last light. But the fact that you were on the ground -- that you were not on the ground at that time impeded on your ability to find out the true story and to identify which units took part in the combat, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. I would accept that, but I would also qualify it by saying if you arrive back to go and visit a unit that was there yesterday and it's gone, you had the intelligence that it's moved. And it pops up somewhere else during the daytime and you find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you have the information to do your job, in terms of convoy protection, but you have no information of who might have attacked such a village.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Not always, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Unless you see it.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Unless I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And also understood -- you also understood that you had an obligation, of course -- sorry that, General Hadzihasanovic had an obligation to guarantee freedom of movement for humanitarian convoys but that no freedom -- he was not under any obligations to give you freedom of movement to look around and gather intelligence.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct. And I therefore focussed on making sure that we were concentrating for a lot of the time on making sure the route was open and clear, because the trucks that were driving down there were driven by civilians, mainly, who were not protected by armour, and therefore it was quite important we had a good picture of what was going on. I often directed my soldiers not to go away from that aid route.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, you were also well aware, of course, that in this context the commanders you were dealing with did not always tell you the truth, or at least not all the truth, as you would have done the same if you had been in their position?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I wasn't in their position; therefore, I can't say whether I would have done that or not. What the commanders told me, we would gather and then sift and compare it with something else. And it was -- you will imagine it -- can imagine, the concept of constructing a jigsaw. You have certain components and you link them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And sometimes, General, a counterpart may give you true information, and in other instances not at all, because they have no -- are under no obligation to reveal secrets as to where they are going to attack.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would just like --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: But at the same time it's sometimes to their advantage to let me know where they were going to attack. Because then we wouldn't be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you also knew that -- you mentioned that all this information that you collected from the people that were deployed and meeting with people, that this was all put into a milinfosum; and that in this case you had Captain Harrison, who would prepare a milinfosum and forward this to many people, amongst others United Nations Central Command in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also knew that all UNPROFOR battalions, your counterparts' battalions, were following the same procedure; that is, the Canadian Battalion was also providing milinfosums and so was the French Battalion and the other battalions in the area.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: They were providing milinfosums, but I was not aware as how they were gathering the information. They may have had a completely different system unique to them as to how they gathered information. I certainly wasn't aware as to whether they had liaison officers talking directly to units. It was their territorial patch and it was therefore not my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, you would agree with me that from the information that was forwarded to BH central command in Kiseljak, a weekly milinfosum would then be produced and forwarded to everyone, including United Nations command in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then from United Nations command in Zagreb the information would come back down in some type of summary form for all the United Nations missions on the ground. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I don't recall getting that feedback, but I'm sure it was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you knew that in parallel to this we had the European Community Monitoring Mission, where the monitors had a similar reporting mechanism from the monitors to coordinating centre, to regional centre, and to ECMM headquarters in Zagreb, and then the same type of information coming back down. Do you recall such a system?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And we had a very close relationship with the ECMM people in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And not only did you have a close relationship; there was also a direct exchange of information between UNPROFOR and ECMM through ECLO, ECLO being the European Community liaison officer. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I don't, actually. I don't recall that at all. Was he a member of the ECMM or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: He was a member of ECMM who was posted with UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Right. Well, I wasn't aware of that existence. We dealt purely on the tactical level with the ECMM teams in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you were able to observe in all the reports that you saw, General, that some incidents were reported more than once.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that some incidents were reported with a different interpretation and that a lot of information was recycled in this way, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. And we took great pains to make sure that our milinfosums had that word "comment." Comment was not fact. Comment was analysis, a thought, an idea. And that was not to be passed on. And if other people were using that as fact, then I'm afraid they got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that was one of my next questions. But in relation to that, you are familiar with the danger that a particular information, a rumour in some cases, might become a belief due to the fact that it is repeated many times in many documents. Are you aware of this danger?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I am. As Shakespeare said, "Rumour is the great traveller." We were extremely careful to make sure that pieces of information that we got were substantiated by other pieces.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do apologise. We made sure that we substantiated the information we were getting in order to build that jigsaw. And a piece of information, no matter how spectacular it might seem at the time, couldn't be really counted on until it was corroborated by other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, those milinfosums in which this information was collated, you mentioned in your statement that you personally reviewed them at night before they were sent out; did you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Either myself or, if I wasn't there, my second-in-command; and if he wasn't there, my senior ops officer, Major Hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Not always yourself?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Not always myself, but there was system to make sure they were reviewed by a senior officer of the battalion, either the second-in-command or the senior major.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So, just because you said you reviewed every single milinfosum, so I was just wondering.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Technically, yes; practically on the ground, I didn't see every single one, but I had a system in place to make sure somebody senior did see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So when Captain Kiggell, or Mr. Kiggell now, stated before the Chamber that the commanding officer may have seen some of the milinfosums before they were dispatched --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- this was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I noticed for the third time today that my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence is quoting from testimony that has been given by other witnesses before this Trial Chamber. I don't think that this is the right manner to proceed, and I do request the Trial Chamber, respectfully do request the Trial Chamber, to instruct my learned friend from the Defence side to not continue with quoting prior testimony of other witnesses before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you mentioned the testimony of witnesses who have already testified before the Tribunal, and you asked the witness what he thought about their testimony. The Prosecution has raised an objection and stated that this is not the way one should proceed, all the more so in that you quote the testimony of witnesses that the witness hasn't seen for years, according to this witness here. And as he wasn't present -- as this witness wasn't present when the testimony was given and he hasn't seen the witnesses for years, is it really a useful and efficient way of proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, there's a direct link between the excerpts from the testimony that I've been using in the course of my cross-examination and the persons who were this witness's subordinates, this witness who is now before the Trial Chamber. And there is no rule against such a procedure - contrary to what my colleague says - because when these persons testified they mentioned a number of events that happened within the BritBat. We now have the BritBat commander before us, and it is quite customary and useful in order to determine the truth to allow the battalion commander to tell us what his impression is, what his opinion is, or to correct certain events related by other witnesses. And the easiest way to do this is to inform him of this testimony. Nevertheless, Mr. President, I will restrict my use of their testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be best to limit your use of the testimony to the minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In English] [Previous translation continues] ... Now, General, coming back on this issue, these milinfosums prepared by your battalion, I believe you said in one of your statements that they were to be considered as snapshots at a particular point in time and that the situation as portrayed in one milinfosum may have changed or evolved in the following days. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. Because otherwise there would be no point in producing a milinfosum every day if you were just repeating the same business. Clearly you wish to reflect events, update your milinfosum, compare the information you've got with the information you're getting, give greater authority to some things that you've said in that you now have them confirmed. It was a living document which went on every day, and we kept them all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And for this reason, General, you mentioned that they should not be considered, that is, the milinfosums, as being the truth at any one time but, rather, the perception of an individual at a specific moment.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's a reasonable statement. I would have been delighted if could produce the absolute truth, but the reality is that doesn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, to come back just quickly on the issue you've mentioned. Wherever the word "comment" appears in those milinfosums, you mentioned that this was not a fact but, rather, a speculation or an educated guess of the person who drafted the report.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, an educated guess gained from his overall picture of seeing all the information come in, his experience in that appointment, his knowledge of what was going on. It is all put together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also said, General, that when you read these comments, you either agreed with them or simply disregarded them because they were not facts.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I didn't -- what, the comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The comments.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The comments were useful for triggering people's minds and thoughts and patterns.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to - again, on this issue of information - because my learned colleague from the Prosecution said or suggested that the milinfosums were a reliable source of information. And it is my understanding that you said yes.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you will agree with me, General, that when we say "reliable source of information," this will depend on the purpose for which the documents are used. Would it not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it would. And they were the best shot at what we believed was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So they may have been reliable to allow you to do your job with the convoys, but they were not reliable in order to identify specifically which unit would conduct an attack at a specific moment.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: If a unit was identified in a milinfosum by its title and because a commander had been met and they were attacking something, that would be put down as fact, and that was reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And this was if an attack was seen by someone.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: And witnessed, et cetera and we knew who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if in the milinfosum we have information that a village is attacked by the ABiH, we don't know which unit was there, do we?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No. And we would probably put "it is attacked by ABiH. Comment: This could probably be Brigade X or Brigade Y."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And brigade X or Brigade X is speculation?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It is comment. As I said, it was speculation on fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when we talk about reliable milinfosum, we must also take into consideration the truth of the information. And if you know that your commanders on the ground may not be telling the truth or are likely hiding from you their operations, then they're not very reliable, are they?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: You're talking both my commanders or the BiH commanders?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The people you meet.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Your liaison officers go out.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: They gather information, and they know, for example, that the information they get might not be accurate.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No. And they weren't only restricted as talking to commanders on the ground. They would move round the area and observe for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: And again, we had a system which I believed at the time was a very efficient method of gathering information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what you mention in this article - and I don't have time to quote it - but you said that you had young liaison officers and that you gave them no directions, in terms of how to gather information.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's correct. Because in the British Army we have a philosophy called "mission command" which says this is what I want you to do and you will do it in the way you find best. And each individual young officer who went out there knew what his task was; how he achieved that task, I left to him. Because the situation he was in at the time, the unit he was trying to find or to report back or the terrain he was in will be completely different. And for me to put down a set standard way of how they got it would be completely wrong. I wanted to know, you know -- you tell me what's going on in that area, how you find that information is up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned in this article also that the information you succeeded in collecting gave you the possibility to anticipate what would happen.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I think -- because I was catching information from HVO and BiH and everybody in that area, particularly of the Lasva Valley, I think I was probably the best informed person in that Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But it --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Because I had many more sources than just the resources of my battalion. I had everything else. And I put it together. And I would suggest that of all the people in that Lasva Valley, my milinfosum crew and myself probably had a pretty good handle on what was going on in the whole area; probably the best of any of the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I'll take your word for it, and we will confirm this with some documents that I will show you, General. But would it not be true that when you arrived on the ground, you were provided with an org chart of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that this org chart by the time you left had been modified on a weekly basis, because even at the end when you left you still could not put together how the 3rd Corps was composed and how the Central Bosnia Operative Zone of the HVO was composed. Is that a precise statement?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It wasn't precise, but we deliberately modified it to keep up with events as we learnt them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, because you gave all this latitude to your liaison officers, some of them ran into difficulties, did they not?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Possibly. And you're going to refer to a specific, I'd be interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And we referred to the specific case of Cameron Kiggell. Now, is it not a fact, General, that why General Hadzihasanovic requested specifically for Mr. Kiggell to be removed and replaced was because Mr. Kiggell was going beyond what he was supposed to do and he was looking and trying to look in military operations and military secrets, and this was mentioned to you by General Hadzihasanovic? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: If General Hadzihasanovic thought my liaison officer was going too far in his, you know, access to the corps, which he effectively had and he said he wanted him removed, I took him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: And actually, Mr. Kiggell at that stage was then moved up to Tuzla, and I put a new lieutenant captain, Andrew Jackson, I believe, came in as a liaison officer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you feel, General, it would have been your responsibility to inform Cameron Kiggell of what he should and should not do so that you would accomplish your mission and maintain an impartial view in this conflict?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: He was aware of the need to be impartial. He was also aware of the need to talk to commanders. And as I said before, I don't tell people how to do things that they take in from the training and the instruction we give them. I tell them what I want to do. If they doesn't work, and they get rejected, we say okay we're not getting the information we expect to get from that area. I'll try somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But isn't the commander responsible for everything?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Ultimately, I was responsible for everything and I will take responsibility for everything that happened with my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on to show to you, because you mentioned you had the best source of information on the ground in the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: At the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: At the time. Now, I'd like to refer you to one document, and that is in the -- the documents that were given to you. This would be, General, the fourth document in your binder. Again I apologise, because I was not able to put the tabs in the information. Now, this report, General, is --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Are we looking at the same report?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is a document by ECMM called "A road for survival in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it is a special report.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I have it now, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in the top right corner, you should see the numbers R, for Romeo, 020-5993.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, this is a report drafted by Ambassador Thebault. You in your article say that Thebault was a French ambassador who was "particularly effective, very clever, able career diplomat but he had a nasty habit of teeing up a meeting and leaving at the last minute for me to chair a crucial debate." Do you recall those words?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: He did that on two occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at this document, General. And let's take a look together to see whether Ambassador Thebault and the ECMM information collection machine had the same reading of the situation as you had. And I quote the first paragraph, where we talk about the total blockade of the roads coming from the south is "since about three months it is most efficient weapon used by the HVO to strangle Central and North Bosnia and to force the Bosnian Muslims to surrender." I bring to your attention, General, that this is 22 July, at a time when you say that the ABiH has the upper hand and is on the offensive. I quote the second paragraph, where it goes on to say: "The economical weapon has greatly contributed to the degradation of the social and political situation in all ethnically mixed areas, raising mistrust amongst the communities." The next paragraph, where we talk: "Due to total lack of fuel and spare parts, the all-industrial system has now collapsed, slowly followed by all the vital infrastructures." The next paragraph: "People are literally desperate, as shown by the last riots in Tuzla around the UNHCR storage." If we move to the next page, it says here: "This situation is clearly one of the major incentives for today's BiH army attacks, securing a road to the sea has become for them an obsession. The failure of the International Community to realise till now the problem and to solve it in enforcing freedom of movement for emergency supplies is used as an excuse for continuing the fight." I move on, General, to the third paragraph, where it says: "But continuing such a road blockade, which is only due to HVO, has also effects on the life conditions of the Bosnian Croats living in Central Bosnia, leading them to desperation and doing something would also have a clear positive interest for a large part of the Croat community." I'd like to move on to the third paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before having a break, which is very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... [In English] Aimed at obtaining concrete, and quick results for the freedom of movement and goods would be a major recommendation." If we move to the next page, where we say: "After several discussions with UNPROFOR BH command their estimation is that the idea is militarily sensible and could be connected to the implementation of safe areas if there were a political impulse." General, I'd like you to comment as to whether this description of the situation is: One, as you saw it when you were in Bosnia on the 22nd of July; and two, that it is a fair representation that is different from what is depicted in your milinfosum information-gathering machine.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: This is a report which was produced, as you said, by Ambassador Thebault. It is produced for, I assume, civil affairs and that sort of line. It is a completely different report to any reports I would produce. It talks about things at the operational and strategic level, which were well above me. It talks about concepts and it talks about ideas. It was presumably generated by Ambassador Thebault for an aim to inform people as to how things are going, and he suggests a number of ideas and initiatives. It is completely different in purpose, layout, intention to a milinfosum, and I don't -- my milinfosum was to achieve my tactical aim; this is a completely different report. And what is in this report will go further in strategic terms than ever I would dream about in my tactical reports.
