And therefore, what is depicted here is a completely different scenario and business to the business of my milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, do you agree that this clearly illustrates the prevailing circumstances in Central Bosnia when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It illustrates a viewpoint from Ambassador Thebault taken as a snapshot at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: And his -- and if we take that he has gathering sources and as I have gathering sources, he will have a jigsaw puzzle as well that he's trying to fill in. It is then a snapshot in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We will stop here, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we taking a break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for technical reasons we shall be having a break and resume our hearing at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maitre Bourgon, we have three-quarters of an hour. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] General, I would like to move on to ask you a few questions in relation to corps operations as they were conducted in Central Bosnia. First I'd like you to confirm that - and I believe you mentioned this a few minutes ago - that when we talk about military operations, they can be classified as tactical, operational, or strategic.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that a corps works at the operational level, of course, with some input at the tactical level and some input at the strategic level, although on a limited basis.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I would qualify that by saying that your aim would be tactical, operational, or strategic. The means you achieve that doesn't necessarily latch exactly to the -- you can't put exactly there. You may achieve an operational effect by one soldier on the ground, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Would you agree with me that the commanding general at the corps level usually looks ahead at the battlefield 96 hours ahead or more?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: At least, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Hence, in normal circumstances, it is difficult for a commanding general of a corps to have a direct influence on the conduct of operations as they take place.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That would be strange if he didn't have a direct effect, because he would have decided how they were going to be done and then put them into place. If they weren't running true to course, he would therefore -- having got feedback and back briefs from his staff, may need to correct them and put them on track.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me make my question a little more precise. After going through this cycle, when the operation is actually taking place, it will be seldom would the corps general intervene in an operation as going on.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: But if it's not going on according to his plan, he would intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, you would agree with me, then, that the corps commander's duty is to translate the strategic objectives that he received from the state and which are communicated to him by army headquarters into operational directives, which will then be accomplished on the ground by, for example, operational groups and brigade commanders so that they know what they have to do.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: If that's how he wishes to command his corps, yes. There are different ways of going that business.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when we talk about the responsibility of any commanding officer, but even more so for a corps commander, I would suggest to you that there are three types of responsibilities: Responsibilities towards the state and the chain of command; responsibilities towards subordinates; and legal responsibilities. Would that cover grosso modo the responsibilities of a commanding general of a corps?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It is brief, yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we look at upward responsibility, this simply means that the army will always be -- will always answer to the political organs of the state, at least in the kind of armies that are in mostly the Western world; and that any commanding officer owes his loyalty first and foremost always upwards towards the chain of command. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. But he has the right to come back on what the chain of command has asked him to do and discuss it, if necessary. And that is enshrined in the British Army tradition of mission command. You do not blindly follow orders. That has never been what we've done in out army, in my army. And that is not what a commander should do. And if you disagree violently with what you have been given to do, you either put up with it or resign.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as far as responsibility towards soldiers or towards subordinates, the loyalty -- some people say there is not even such a thing as loyalty, but there is a responsibility to ensure that the soldiers will make it alive after battle ask that that really the responsibility of the commanding general. Would you agree with such a statement?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: He cannot guarantee that soldiers will be alive after the battle, but it's in his plan he should aim to produce a plan that has the minimum impact upon his own troops in terms of death, and wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with respect to legal responsibilities, you will agree with me, General, that as in the specific circumstances we are dealing with, that General Hadzihasanovic, as a commanding general, had to abide by national laws, by international laws, and also by the directives within his own army?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. And I would add that he should also abide by his own ethical guidelines and moral philosophy as to what is right and what is wrong with what he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, would you agree with me that when we talk about the responsibilities of a commanding general towards the chain of command, towards subordinates, as well as legal responsibilities, there is one word that comes back and that can join the three together, and that is "discipline"? Would you agree with this statement?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I think it's a rather wide statement, but if you wish to make it, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree that maintaining discipline within a military unit will allow the unit to accomplish its mission; it will allow for the soldiers to protect themselves; and it will also allow to avoid violations of the law?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'd accept those.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in terms of a commander, his responsibility with respect to discipline is to ensure that any violations of the law are taken care of; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in such circumstances -- it may be disciplinary violations or it may be criminal acts, what is important is that the commander wants his soldiers to abide by the law; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I'd agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And things such as, for example, desertion or leavings -- or leaving one's post, leaving one's duty during wartime, those are very serious offences, which in peacetime would not have the same meaning.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if we talk about stealing a bag of flour or -- simply, the offence of stealing would be as important if you're talking about stealing a fellow member of your force or stealing in the civilian world. Stealing is bad and both of them are as bad.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. But they should be taken each individual case on its merits and to do entirely pertinent the circumstances prevailing at that time. So it would be impossible to say one is equally bad. Yes, stealing in general is bad; but you would have to be specific time, place, intention, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So the prevailing circumstances at the time are indeed very important when we talk about discipline.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you must be familiar, General, with -- when we conduct military operations, with what is called "the principles of war."

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that there are 10, 11, or 9, depending on the army, but that there's one which is the most important principle of war, and I take it that that this is the one that is the most important in your army, that is, the army of the United Kingdom, and that is selection and maintenance of the aim.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I have had over the years many discussions on the composition of the principles of war, which is more important and which isn't. I wouldn't select any particular one, because they are pertinent to circumstances. The selection and maintenance of the aim is important to achieve your aim at the end of the day, but I'm not saying it's overriding. There may be other conditions that undermine it or make it impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you take General Hadzihasanovic with the mission that he was given, would you agree with me that his focus at the time should have been selection and maintenance of the aim and that the mission was --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I do not know what his mission is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I propose to you that General Hadzihasanovic's mission was: One, to hold the line against the Serb forces; two, to create a corps, which was non-existent; and three, to create the necessary conditions to put a force together which can be used to free Sarajevo, would you agree with me that in the circumstances ruling at the time General Hadzihasanovic, it was his duty to focus on his mission?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, and you've told me what his mission is. And I wasn't aware of the requirement to free Sarajevo, but I would say that he was particularly success informal the first two elements of that mission; that is, to hold the line against Serb forces and to create a corps, which is non-existent. Those were achieved with huge success.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, we had an expert witness not too long ago before this Chamber. I'm not going to quote his words. But there's an issue that was discussed then which I would like to put to you, and that is the difference between accountability and criminal responsibility. I would like to propose to you that there is a difference between the two, and to use your example, your example being you are, or you were, the commander of the BritBat; as the commander of BritBat, you were responsible for everything that related to BritBat. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as such, you were accountable and if you do -- if you did a good job, you would be promoted, and if you did a bad job, you would not be promoted, or there could be various other circumstances; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President. Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects to such line of questioning. It's very obvious that my learned friend from the Hadzihasanovic Defence is asking questions to this witness which an expert witness should be asked. He's using this witness as a sort of a second expert. And I point out what I already did recently: There's a difference -- there's a huge difference between two situations. The first situation is that we have a fact witness who was on the ground, testifies on facts, and based on his or her expertise is in a position to draw conclusions on the facts he or she has seen. What my learned friend from the Defence is now doing, he's using this witness who is a fact witness as a pure expert. The line of questioning we have seen for the last two minutes are not related to the facts on the ground. These are purely theoretical questions an expert should be asked, and I object against this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The objection raised by the Prosecution relates to the fact that we have a fact witness and we're not dealing with an expert witness here. Mr. Bourgon, what do you have to answer with regard to this objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question which is asked to the witness is not something which is a question relating -- which would be asked to an expert witness. It's a question I ask him because he was a commander of the BritBat in that region in 1993. So it was a question relating to the fact and pertaining to his military knowledge of the situation. Therefore, I think it should be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that your question should be put against the backdrop of a more general context. I think he did say during his testimony that he was in charge of training all the soldiers of the British Army that are being sent to theatres of war outside their country, and therefore he's entitled to these questions. A question of a general nature, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, I would ask you to, in light of the comments made by the Presiding Judge of the Trial Chamber, whether you agree generally with the fact that commanders are responsible generally for everything that takes place in their unit.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And they are accountable for what goes on, and if something does go wrong, it may lead to consequences which may be related to career measures or administrative measures.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: They are accountable, but I think to trace a line of consequences to career or administrative is one of a number of scenarios you could paint. But I don't think it's linked. Yes, we are responsible; yes, we are accountable. Full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when we talk about accountability, General, you will agree with me that there is a distinction with your criminal liability and that in the case of a commanding officer who has not committed himself any offences, that his criminal liability should only be involved when there is on his part gross negligence amounting to personal dereliction of duty. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that criminal liability doesn't apply until a certain thing happens? Because criminal liability is there whatever with a commanding officer. It doesn't go away. And it starts from the word go. And I'm -- if I as a commanding officer make a criminal action, I am responsible and accountable for that. It doesn't switch on and off. It's something that is there at all time. The behaviour of your army if you're an army commander; if you're a battalion commander, if the behaviour of my battalion. It's my responsibility and I'm accountable. That doesn't go away. You can't switch it on and off. It's there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is exactly my point, General. If a commanding officer commits offences, and you've seen that happen before because you testified in the trial of General Blaskic who was found guilty for ordering an unlawful attack on civilians. He committed a violation and he was found guilty for his participation in this violation. You are aware of this fact.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm aware he was found guilty. I'm not aware of the details, apart from the evidence I gave at the time on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, has the Prosecution in this case explained to you the difference between this case and the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No, and I wouldn't expect them do, because this case stands on its own. And I think making linkages is -- you've got to be very careful about. Different force, different army, different people, different mission, different tasks. If you're trying to chuck everything together and get something out of it, I think that's wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, from a legal perspective, I take it, then, that the Prosecution did not explain to you that in this specific case General Hadzihasanovic was not accused for having committed any crime, participated in any crime, planning any crime, instigating any crime, aiding any crime, or abetting in any crime? Did the Prosecution explain that to you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I suggest to you now that the difference between this trial and another trial, not on the facts, because I agree that you don't want to mingle the facts - Blaskic is Blaskic; General Hadzihasanovic is a completely different matter - but as a matter of legal responsibility, General Hadzihasanovic is accused for violations which were allegedly committed by subordinates, not for his own violations. Do you understand the difference?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I understand that. And I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, given that General Hadzihasanovic is accused for violations committed by subordinates and not for his own, would you agree with me that in such a case the question is whether, in line with what you said earlier, General Hadzihasanovic acted reasonably in the circumstances prevailing at the time.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: If, as you say, General Hadzihasanovic is here to answer to the actions of his subordinates, then what his subordinates did he is both responsible and accountable for, because that the duty of a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I understand, General. But my question to you is: To what extent is he criminally responsible if your subordinate committed a violation and committed theft, you would not want to be responsible for theft, would you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: But I am responsible for making sure something is done about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: And it's not swept under the carpet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: And if -- and if it proves in the system that it -- my criminal negligence that has resulted in that theft, then I'm responsible for that. And you can't switch that off.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you agree with me, then, General, that the difference in this case is that -- the accusation is that General Hadzihasanovic did not take the necessary and reasonable measures in the circumstances to punish or prevent. That's the accusation. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that given that we are talking about the necessary and reasonable measures, that what we are talking about is we are talking about the exercise of command by General Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I would agree with that, but I would say again that that exercise of command covers everything. A commander, as you've said before, is responsible for the actions of his troops, the way they behave, and he's accountable for that as well. I will keep coming back to that, because you are accountable. I am accountable for the way my current command behaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, if he took the necessary and reasonable measures in the circumstances prevailing at the time - and we discussed this - then he should not be criminally responsible. You understand the difference?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I do understand the difference. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, let me move on to the vertical responsibility, chain of command. You will agree with me that the chain of command will go from the lowest level up to the highest level in what we call unity of command and vertical chain of command.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that if a soldier commits a breach, it is not every commander at every level that will be responsible or that will be found guilty of this breach? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I would agree with that. But I would also add that it's important -- right from the very top, there is a transparent system that we know works and is in place and enforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, you will agree with me that this vertical chain of command means that different commanders at different levels have different responsibilities regarding a fact which is committed by a soldier.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you don't expect the company commander to have the same implications with regards to a breach committed by a soldier than the corps commander or the army commander.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: He will have a responsibility to that company commander to make sure that the system in place is adhered to and followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: And if he fails to follow that system which is adhered to and in place, then he is in breach.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, if the general -- if the commanding general of a corps did take the necessary measures to put the system in place, to give the necessary orders, and if he has fulfilled his responsibilities at his level, then you will agree with me that he should not be found criminally responsible.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Provided he has put in -- not only put the system in place but he has checks and balances to ensure that the system he has put in place is working, is practical, and has worked throughout. It is no good just putting a system in place and stepping back and saying, "Hey, I've done it. Not my problem." Wrong. You put a system in place and you make very, very sure that that system is workable, manageable, et cetera, et cetera. You can't just leave it to lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, when the commanding general does take action, does put the system in place, we spoke earlier of the trust amongst the chain of command. It is not, you will agree with me, for the commanding general to go and look all the way down where the soldier has committed the breach to find out if something went wrong unless he is being informed by his chain of command that something went wrong. Will you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I will agree. But you've got to make sure he has a system in place to make sure his chain of command reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely, General. That's exactly my point.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: And he needs to check up on that. And he does needs to go with his telescope and poke down. He is responsible for everything in it. If he is not happy with the system, he should change it to make it work. If there is a risk that he has exposed, then he should fill that gap.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, when the commanding general is leading a war and he is involved in the kind of situation we are talking about - and you know all the obligations that we are talk about in terms of leading a war, planning the activities, directing the activities - and then you will agree with me that the commanding general, if he did take all the measures that were necessary in the circumstances at his level and that -- then he should not be found criminally responsible.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: So what you are saying is that if it's a very intense war and it's all a bit busy, he can just forget some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: You just said he's a very busy commander, he's planning, directing the rest of it. And you're saying this somehow changes circumstances. I'm sorry, it doesn't. You have the responsibility. It doesn't matter whether you are doing peace support operations in one state, Northern Ireland, you have the responsibilities of the command. You can't wish it away because circumstances are difficult. You can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But the test, you will agree with me, General, is necessary and reasonable measures in the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Provided you have a system that's made sure they're realistic. If you haven't put -- if you personally haven't got a system that work, then -- then that you are to blame for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, if I indicate to you -- and you mention that you were aware of the disciplinary law in force in Bosnia, were you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Military of civilian?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Military. In the way for General Hadzihasanovic to deal with any violations inside the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I believe there was a code of conduct published by 3rd Corps. I didn't see it, but I believe there was a code of conduct, because I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you're not aware of any mechanism that was made that was put in place, are you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I am aware that certain mechanisms were put in place by the 3rd Corps because they wanted to make sure they had those mechanisms in place. And I believe that the then-Colonel Hadzihasanovic was very diligent in putting those things in place, to make sure that they happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you know that General Hadzihasanovic did put a system in place. Now, did you know that this system was a three-level system which was disciplinary offences within the units, which was disciplinary court within the corps, which was a military court which was separated from the 3rd Corps, and that was also a special military court that would entitle a brigade commander to sentence one of his soldiers to death? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of the penalties involved, no. I was purely aware that there was a code in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you aware, General, that during the time that General Hadzihasanovic was commanding the 3rd Corps there were more than 1.000 criminal reports which were filed from the chain of command, from the lowest level up to his level, more than 1.000 criminal reports were filed at all levels following the orders issued by General Hadzihasanovic? Were you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: There's no reason why I would know of it and I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you would be aware of this and you know the circumstances in which General Hadzihasanovic was operating, would you agree with me that this was a commander -

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You'll have to -- Can you please ask me that again because I haven't heard it because the interpreter interrupted. We're going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, it's my mistake. I was speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, if I simply tell you that in the circumstances ruling at the time, and we both agree, that a commander cannot forget what is going on; right? We agree?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I tell you that in what was going on in Bosnia General Hadzihasanovic issued a number of orders which led to more than 1.000 criminal complaints filed against members of the 3rd Corps, does that indicate to you and would that be not surprising to you given all the qualities that you've mentioned about General Hadzihasanovic as a commander?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I was not aware that that number of cases were brought up and documented. But you're going back on this -- you're taking the scale of the thing and saying that excuses everything. To me that is the line that coming across from you. You are saying different circumstance, really different, lots and lots of complaints, and therefore it doesn't matter. Now, if there were lots of complaints, I'm afraid you have to move to put things in place. The situation has changed. And has the commander, you must recognise the situation has changed. There is a problem. I do not have an efficient system of dealing with these complaints because there are so many. I must put something in place and I must do it now because otherwise it will bite me in the back later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if you -- if the commander is seen to take such measures, then he is fulfilling his responsibility as a corps commander.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Provided the measures he takes are effective, can be enforced, and are policed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes. So we agree that if he takes such measures and is seen to take such measures by issuing the orders, by complaining against a court system that is not his, that he is taking all the measures that are possible at the time to ensure that violations are prevented taken and punished.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I am not qualified to comment on the Bosnian Military Code and whether he had taken the appropriate measures because I don't know what they were and I'm not qualified to answer that. But unless -- the system has failed because of that, then the system needs adjustment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what I'm saying to you, General, is that you've met General Hadzihasanovic many times. You mentioned a lot of qualities about him. And you mentioned that he did act diligently to put a lot of things in place. Now, in such circumstances, if I tell you that he did take measures to enforce discipline, without going into the measures, would you be surprised knowing the man?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I would not be surprised. I would expect him to have taken measures to enforce discipline. And I'm sure he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, if we move on to the fact of the situation on the ground. And if I talk about -- you knew that the -- where you were fighting was Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you knew that this territory or if there was one governmental army or governmental forces, that was the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Are you saying that was the only army in -- the only army? That was the state army?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That was the army or the legitimate army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was only one. And that was the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. I was only aware of the fact that when I got there there were three armies fighting, Serbs, Croats, and effectively Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you were not aware that actually the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was defending its own territory, like if you would be defending London, against rebel groups inside the state? Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I understood that. But if you take the view that it was taken from the Bosnian-Herzegovinian army, you can take the same view if you talk about the Serbs or the Croats. This was --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But General --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: And I'm not saying it's all the same. I'm not saying that the whole thing is neat little boxes. What I'm saying is that when I arrived there, there were three warring armies. Their war was something I had to put up with and was in my cases obstructing my aim. But that's what I've been sent to do, to get the aid through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what you're telling me --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I was not going to be able to influence the outcome of that war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So what you are telling me, General, is that to you it made no difference whether the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was on the defensive defending its territory against two aggressors who had been declared illegal by the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That did not matter to you.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: At the time it did not matter, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you understood that in part of this conflict there was initially the Serbs, who were the aggressor against the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was working with the HVO. You understood that.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that. And clearly I had been briefed on the events that had come to get to the situation that I found myself in Bosnia at the time. But you are now talking about business. I was a battalion commander in the Lasva Valley. I was collecting information to make sure that I could get my aid through.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. That's what I wanted to get from you, in terms of information. Now, when we look at the facts of the case, you will agree with me that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was a new army that was created in November of 1993. By the time you got there, this army was less than eight months old. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I knew it was a new army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you knew that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not have weapons, did not have access because of the embargo to any weapons, unlike the HVO; because you do mention this in your statement, that the HVO did get access to some weapons.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you knew that the roads in the Lasva Valley were completely blocked, in terms of the Lasva Valley and Central Bosnia with you actually under siege with no access to the sea, no access to the south, and no access to the north.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: For the Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Muslims. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you provided a third statement to the Office of the Prosecution talk about the issue of refugees. You are able to testify that the issue of refugees was indeed a very important issue which created lots of problems for all the people there, but especially for the commander of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you please -- because I needs to have your --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that, because the number of refugees were coming into his area of control and he clearly had to look after them and made sure they had shelter as best he could.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, can you confirm that in Gornji Vakuf and area, there was fighting throughout your stay in Bosnia, there was fighting before and fighting continued after you left? Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, except there was quite a lull for about three months, I think. There was certainly fighting before, with the regiment before. There was only a break, and then we had a lot of fighting towards the end of my time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in one of the documents that was shown to you, General, you mentioned the Maglaj finger, and you mentioned that as of July the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was moving -- at least that they were -- there was a shift in the operational tempo where they were on the offensive.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Were you able to see what happened to the Maglaj finger from the time you arrived to the time you left and that as a matter of fact the complete Maglaj finger was taken, that this territory was lost to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that this created a serious strategic and operational problem for the state as a whole? Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I am certainly aware of the changes of the military dispositions in the Maglaj finger during the time I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you -- based on your reading of the geography of Central Bosnia, did you understand that if there was to be a solution to this conflict, in terms of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it could only come from Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No. I didn't understand that. There was no reason day to day where I would start to think about these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, in one of your milinfosums - and I will show you to you in a minute - you did mention that you could not understand the difference in situation between 2 Corps and 3 Corps, whereas in 2 Corps they seemed to be friends and in 3 Corps it's like as if they are enemies and we are at a loss to understand that. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: What I was surprised at was in my understanding 2 Corps consisted of HVO and BiH units, who seemed to be fighting side by side up in the north in the Tuzla area. But I didn't understand why down in the Lasva Valley area we'd had this huge split and rift between the HVO and the BiH. That difficult to comprehend how, you know, part of the country you've got people fighting side by side and yet further south they're at odds with each other. That was difficult to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if we think about Vares, you mentioned the fact that -- or in response to a question that the General took some leave in the later part. You didn't belief General Hadzihasanovic, did you, when he told you that he was going to see his family?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Well, I had no reason not to believe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But that -- in your report then you say that there was something else.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: When he's been seen going into 2 Corps? That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you understand at that point why he went to 2 Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I can understand why he went to 2 Corps. And I have no problem with the BiH's military plan and the actions they took. The problem may come in the way they've done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: All I'm saying is that whatever war plans 3 Corps had, they executed them and that was absolutely fine. I do not have a problem with that. The fact that they managed to overcome the initial dominance of the HVO was acceptable. I'm not -- that's not a problem. This was their war which they were conducting and they were conducting, I thought, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, did you understand --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: But we are here on the business, and you keep coming back to this. You can sort of strike off because it's all too difficult..

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, did you understand that when talk about Vares --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because you mentioned that --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- also, Vares was an important objective, it was actually a strategic objective, and that without taking Vares the risk was losing in the same way they had lost the Maglaj finger, as you called it, and cutting completely the north. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I did understand that, and I also understood, and I was shown, a route round to avoid Vares in order to enable a link-up, as it were, without using the Vares route.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: So it was an attempt to go round the Vares route.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, you mention in your statement the cooperation between the Serbs and the HVO. You were conscious of this, were you?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when we talk about human superiority or soldier superiority of the ABiH, in terms of numbers over the HVO, that is discounting the fact that the HVO was working with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure the point you're trying to make there. Because what I am saying is that I thought the BiH were extremely well motivated. They did not have outside assistance as the Serbs and the Croats had, and it was quite amazing what they managed to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, you will agree with me that in terms of the number of troops, we have the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which may have been superior in numbers to the HVO; but if you put the HVO and the Serbs together, it was not superior in number, was it?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: No. But that's just a mathematical thing with the three warring factions there. You can put it any way you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, were you aware that -- because you don't mention this very much in all of your statements -- that General Hadzihasanovic had to keep up more than 300 kilometres of front line with the Serbs in his own area of operations?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: And I had a front line from Tuzla down to Romboci which was about 300 kilometres. And I had to put up with that the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you compare your responsibilities as a BritBat commander with holding the line against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I don't compare them at all. You've mentioned a scale saying it's 300 kilometres, which is unusual for a corps. I mentioned then to you that I was given an area of 300 kilometres, which is unusual for me. I'm not comparing the two, I'm just saying -- you know, these things happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Do you realise, General that having 300 kilometres of front line to hold against the Serbs was very demanding on the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina both on the General, on the commanding general, but in terms of numbers of soldiers to man this line?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I wouldn't deny that at all and I haven't denied it and I've said they did a fantastic job.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, General, when we talk about the fact that this line was at one point manned jointly by the HVO and the ABiH and that as the HVO was pulling out and leaving the line, that created very big difficulties for the commanding general.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes. And I saw that when -- I believe in the Travnik area a whole HVO unit pulled out and very quickly, the BiH in that area had to fill that gap. And I know for a fact that the HVO walked straight round into Serb hands and came back down south again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to show you three documents before we end for today. And the first one, I'd like to look at the documents number 5 in your -- the fifth document in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, we have three minutes until we should adjourn. How much time do you need for your documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have three documents, Mr. President. And it will take me five minutes to deal with them. I'll then have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... Document in your binder, and this is a document dated the 6th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Is that the number 03041866?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, that the document.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: All right. I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you just read the first paragraph below the word "order," where it says: "Having seen for myself the state of communications in units and the wasteful and non-functional use of available means at the operative group level and the partial concealing of some equipment and with the aim of better functioning and establishing an integrated communications system, I hereby order." This paragraph, General, does that indicate to you that communications were as good as you say so?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It indicates to me that the commander, Mehmed Alagic, who I assume signed at the bottom and that's his -- has decided that he's got a problem and he's put a team to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It's merely the level.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: What described by the commander may be very different on the ground. Perhaps he's not happy as an ops group but he hasn't got the communications he might need on the basis that the ops group has just been formed. I don't know. You are taking a document, one document and trying to put it in -- and I'm trying to put it in a context, which is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: One man's view of poor communications may not be the view of the next man.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you say you don't know, General, actually you did not know when you were there the state of communications down to the company, the battalion, and the brigade level. You did not know.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: When I went and was stopped at a -- a crossing by military police because I was going to visit the then-Colonel Hadzihasanovic, they phoned through and yes, I went through and they allowed me to get through. On a number of occasions we could get a very quick reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, General, I'd like to refer you to document number 3, the third document on your list, dated 21 August. And I would like to quote page 10.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This is a document -- this is a report that was sent by the commander of the 3rd Corps, General Hadzihasanovic, to his superior headquarters to say exactly the state of the 3rd Corps in August. If we look on page 10, "Command and control problems." The first paragraph states: "Command and control problems are complex and at this stage of the execution of combat operations they are the result of consequences of three very important factors: Competence of personnel, communications equipment, and motivation." Does that indicate to you that communication is a problem within the 3rd Corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It -- well, I don't know the context in this was written. I see the date is August. I don't know what the whole report says or what the report conclusions came to. But the sentence you have picked out states that he believes -- or that the author believes there is a problem with communications, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And with that sentence, General, would you also say that motivation that you thought was very, very strong also appears at least to be a problem?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It appears to be. But my perception from reports gathered in my area from the ground told me that the motivation was pretty high.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if I go down this page, General, to the last paragraph, where it talks about communications more specifically and where it says: "Another problem is communications equipment in the command and control system. This problem again exists at the lower levels, that is, at the squad, platoon, and company levels. So, for instance, a company is carrying out an attack or organising defence and the company commander does not have radio or wire communications with the platoon commanders but only courier communication." Does that indicate to you, without going into more details, that communications was not all that good in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Well, no, because I turn over the page and I see that "Notwithstanding --" if you turn to page 11; yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: It says "not withstanding the following types of communication have been established." And there is a list of communications which are working. There is a list, as I said, and this the first I've ever seen of it -- and there is a list of communication planned and established and more planned and established. So that was taken to improve that even before this report was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, this General, is what you would expect of a competent general like General Hadzihasanovic because his responsibility to work towards establishing a communications system.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, and it's apparent for me that General Hadzihasanovic has put in place a process to sort this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And one last question --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I would ask whether that process has been transferred to other areas to sort it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: General, a big issue was made out of the satellite phone which was used or which -- the number which was given. Can you confirm that this number was given to you by Mr. Merdan?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you confirm, General, that you did not know that this satellite phone was actually the satellite phone of the Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was exceptionally put at the disposal of General Hadzihasanovic because he was expecting communications from his superior headquarters? Did you know this fact?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: That doesn't alter the fact that the communications is there. If I've been given a phone number to ring, I'll use it. I'm not bothered whether it's Vodaphone, some other cell not working. If it work, I'll use it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Where it comes from is immaterial. The communication link was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And General, one last question. If we talk about a satellite phone like this, you understand that in order to communicate with anyone you must have another satellite phone?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: You maybe had one, but nobody else had one in Bosnia; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: The various liaison officer teams had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In your --

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because you had the equipment.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: But we stilled that that link --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But not equipment inside the 3rd Corps for command and control purposes.

utterances.speaker: ALASTAIR DUNCAN
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have finished for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, yesterday you were not in the courtroom, but we discussed the length of the testimony which could be carried over tomorrow, and you have mentioned that you needed two hours, you will -- the Defence team has required two hours all in all, because we did say that we had to discuss the issue of the documents after the hearing. In other words, how much time will you require tomorrow to complete your cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had 30 minutes tomorrow, I'd be very happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about the other Defence counsels?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I might only require a very short time, no more than five to ten minutes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General. I'm sure you've understood that the hearing is not finished for today, fortunately or unfortunately, I don't know. You will have to stay overnight and come back tomorrow morning and be here at 9.00 in this courtroom. So we shall proceed with the rest of the cross-examination tomorrow at of 9.00 onwards tomorrow morning. And I shall ask the usher to accompany you outside the courtroom and ask you to be here tomorrow morning at 9.00, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, since we anticipate that tomorrow we will have the continuing discussion on documents, I wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel to the fact that we today filed the further detailed consolidated Prosecution exhibit list in chronological order containing all the information the Chamber requested by its order of 29th of April. The exhibit list is filed in an A3 format for the only purpose to make it readable to all parties involved. It may be helpful for the tomorrow's discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the Defence team has noted the fact that the Prosecution has prepared a document in line with the instructions we had given on the filing of documents. So we will be able, if necessary, to use this A3 format document, which I have not seen yet. If there are no further issues to be raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So our legal assistant has stated that this is an A3 format document. We will not be able to have these documents in a paper format tomorrow, Mr. Withopf, unless you were able to make a copy in paper. I shall give you the floor back. It will be difficult otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This is exactly what I'm going to say, Your Honours. The Prosecution is very willing and prepared to provide both the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel with a copy of this document later on this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So Mr. Bourgon I'm sure will agree with your suggestion. That will avoid him having to turn to the electronic version of the document. Thank you, Mr. Withopf. That said, I shall now adjourn and ask you to come back tomorrow morning at 9.00, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 14th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.52 p.m.,
